s01.slug: MONDAY · 6:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — THE LIST
body: The sun has got as far as the top of the eucalyptus outside 412 and no farther, and the leaves up there have gone a clean, hard yellow, the yellow of the inside of a pear. Below that line the tree is still in shadow and still dripping from the courtyard sprinklers. Down the hall a shower has been going since twenty to seven. The thirteenth day of Lent, and the cold coming in round the window frame is the dry kind that means clear by nine.

Jack has been awake since before the alarm, sitting up on his bed in a T-shirt with the five-subject notebook on his knees, open to its back page, the Oceanography handouts tucked in behind it. He is writing a list. The only lists he has ever made were Nonna’s groceries — escarole, the good provolone, the Folgers in the red can, *not the blue one* — and this one has a heading, and numbers down the side, like an estimate for a roof. It is for no one’s eyes but his.

body.title: Notebook, back page
body.text: PROPERLY — 1. reservation · 2. jacket · 3. iron something (Ma) · 4. flowers · 5. cab · 6. pay

body: He looks it over. He has written it in pen. Pen is a commitment. Five things to do and one to remember. Number four he will need help with; the only flowers he knows anything about are the carnations at the Sparkle Market, and those are for funerals and Mother’s Day. Number three has Ma’s name after it because it’s a direct quote; he has never ironed anything, and Ma, who would iron a dish towel if it held still, will ask.

Across the gap between the beds Theo has one eye open. He is on his side with half his face in the pillow and the sheet pulled up to his ear, and he is reading the notebook upside down. For Theo, before seven in the morning, this is an athletic event.
“You’ve written *pay* on a list.”
“It’s a reminder.”
“It’s a confession.” Theo shuts the eye, turns over to face the wall and pulls the sheet up over his head, and the matter is closed.

The envelope is in the top drawer of the desk, under the Baltimore Catechism: a bank envelope gone soft at the corners, one of Gloria’s gumbands doubled round it. Since January, whatever comes to him out of the tip jar at the end of a shift has gone in there unlooked-at. He counts it now on the blanket, quietly, for Theo’s sake: ones, mostly, and fives, and one twenty folded into quarters by somebody who meant it as a secret. A hundred and sixty-two dollars. He has never eaten anywhere that wanted a jacket. He has no idea what number six costs at a place like that, only that it’s his to cover.

Doing the gumband back up, he notices his hands. They’re better than last week. They put the gumband on and quit, and lie on the blanket like anybody’s hands, and don’t go off looking for anything on their own. The want is still in there somewhere, and it has been getting smaller, a dog that has learned which rooms it isn’t allowed in.

The Carhartt hangs on its hook on the back of the door. On his way out to the shower, towel over his shoulder, he touches the breast pocket going by. The pack is there — the Marlboro Reds from El Paso, cellophane on, seal unbroken, the corners going soft — and he keeps walking.

When he comes back wet-haired, Theo hasn’t moved and the sun has come a foot down the eucalyptus. Jack dresses, and shuts the notebook on the list, and puts a Bic in his back pocket. Number one is a phone number he doesn’t have yet, out of a phone book that lives in the Delgado lobby, and he stands in the middle of 412 with his boots on, trying out in his head how a person says *a table for two* to a stranger without sounding like he’s asking for a loan.

s02.slug: MONDAY · 11:05 AM · HOLLIS HALL, THE FRONT STEPS — PARTY OF TWO
body: The front steps of Hollis face south and hold the sun, and by eleven on a clear Monday half the philosophy department is out on them with coffee, pretending to read. Out past the library a mower starts up, does the length of something, and quits.

Jack has the top step, out of the traffic, with the RAZR open in his hand: the hinge cold, the crack across the little outside screen throwing a splinter of light up at him. The number is on the back of his left hand in blue Bic, where it has been since a quarter past seven; all morning he has kept that hand out of his pockets.

body.text: He found it in the Delgado lobby’s Yellow Pages under *Restaurants*: the place Gloria put at the end of the wharf. *Le Marin*, a quarter-page, with a little anchor drawn in the corner and *Jackets Required* set underneath in italics, as if it were part of the address.
body.else: He found it in the Delgado lobby’s Yellow Pages under *Restaurants — Fine Dining*, of which Marisol has two, and picked the one on the water: *Le Marin*, a quarter-page, with a little anchor drawn in the corner and *Jackets Required* set underneath in italics, as if it were part of the address.

body.text: She said yes to Saturday under an olive tree, in a sprinkler, to a real place with tablecloths. This is the real place.
body.else: He has decided Saturday is the night he’ll ask her to. He means to have the table first; he isn’t going to invite her to a place he hasn’t got.

body: He had it worked out on the walk over. *Hi, I’d like to make a reservation for two on Saturday at seven-thirty, the name is Costigan.* One sentence, everything in it, no openings for anybody to ask him anything. He said it twice crossing the quad. At home you don’t reserve; you go to the Golden Dawn and stand by the register till a booth comes open. The ad says *Reservations from 11 a.m.*, so at eleven exactly he dialed, and got eleven rings and nobody, and sat on the step with the shut phone against his chin while the girl beside him highlighted Kant in long, violent strokes. He gave them till five past. He has never once given anybody till five past. On the third ring of the second try somebody picks up, and it goes otherwise at once.
“Le Marin, good morning.” A man’s voice, unhurried, with a room behind it: a glass set down on glass, a radio somewhere low, a laugh in a kitchen.
“Morning. Hi. I’d like — for Saturday. Seven-thirty. If you have it. Two.”
“Saturday the sixth, seven-thirty, for two.” A page turns, a big one, the sound of a book that lives on a stand. “We do. And the name?”
“Costigan.”
“Costigan.” The man tries it out. “With a *K*?”
“With a *C*. C-O-S — ”
“C-O-S,” the man says, writing.

“ — T-I-G-A-N.” Two sophomores go down the steps past his knees with their coffee. He is on the front steps of a philosophy building with the entire alphabet at his disposal, and to make sure of it he says, “*C* as in *Catholic*.”

There’s a pause on the line, short, with a smile in it somewhere that the man is too well brought up to let into his voice. “*C* as in *Catholic*,” he says. “I have it.” And then, in the same pleasant tone, a fact about the weather: “Gentlemen are required to wear a jacket, sir.”
“Yes, sir.”
It comes out the way Frank says it to a state trooper on the shoulder of 680, and it’s too late to get it back.
“So: Saturday,” the man says, reading it over, “seven-thirty — ”
“Saturday, seven-thirty,” Jack says along with him, and turns on the step, and Lena is coming up the steps behind him.

She has a stack of library books against her chest and a yellow pencil stuck through the knot of her hair, and her medal out over her sweater where the sun can find it, and her eleven o’clock must have let out at the door, because here she is. She has heard. She puts her eyes front, lifts her chin, and comes on up past him without changing her pace by a hair.
“I heard nothing,” she says, going by. “I’m a vault.”
The door of Hollis takes her, and swings to.
He stands on the top step with the phone at his ear and all the blood in his body gone up into his face, and the girl with the Kant, without lifting her highlighter, says, “Smooth.”
“Sir?”
“Sorry. Still here.”
“Will this be a special occasion?”

Jack looks at the door. On the far side of it are the stairs, and somewhere on them, her. *A special occasion.* He has been asked that once in his life, at a steakhouse out in Boardman the night he was confirmed, and Ma answered for the table. Ma isn’t here. The man on the line waits with his pen. He sounds prepared to wait till lunch.

choices.text: “Yes.”
response: “Yes.”
It is all he’s got, and the man on the line seems to find it sufficient. “Very good, Mr. Costigan.” A pen on paper, a long way off. Jack shuts the phone and goes in after her.

response.text: Hollis climbs in short flights round a well of worn brown linoleum, and at the first turn, where the landing goes out of sight of the lobby, she is waiting on the step above with her books against her chest. She kisses him without a word — quick, easy, a thing she does now, since Sunday on his step, as though they’d been at it for years — and goes up the last flight ahead of him.
response.else: Hollis climbs in short flights round a well of worn brown linoleum, and at the first turn, where the landing goes out of sight of the lobby, she is waiting on the step above with her books against her chest. She kisses him without a word, quick, the two of them a little surprised by how easy it is, and goes up the last flight ahead of him.

response: The Hollis machine’s coffee is on his mouth now, from hers, and he can still feel exactly where the corner of a library book dug into him. He wouldn’t have moved it for money.
He climbs it after her with his hand on the banister where hers was.

choices.text: “It’s a first date.”
response: “It’s a first date.”

On the line the pen stops, and starts again, slower. “A first date,” the man repeats, as though it were a very good year. “Very good, Mr. Costigan.” Jack has said it out loud, to a stranger, on the front steps of the philosophy building. The girl with the Kant goes on highlighting. He shuts the phone with his face going warm.

response.text: He takes the Hollis stairs after her, and at the first turn, where the landing goes out of sight, she is waiting one step up, so that for once they’re the same height. She kisses him, quick — since Sunday it’s a thing she simply does — and says “Vault,” against the corner of his mouth, and goes on up.
response.else: He takes the Hollis stairs after her, and at the first turn, where the landing goes out of sight, she is waiting one step up, so that for once they’re the same height. She kisses him, quick, both of them startled by how easy it turns out to be, and says “Vault,” against the corner of his mouth, and goes on up.

response: She has done it with one hand on the banister and the other arm full of books, nothing but her mouth. It turns out to be plenty.
He stays on the landing a minute with his ears gone hot.

choices.text: “It’s a form.”
response: “It’s a form.”

“A form, sir.” The pen goes, briefly. Jack would put the whole envelope on the word *form* being in that book now, in good ink, beside his name. “Very good, Mr. Costigan.” Jack has a feeling the man is going to enjoy Saturday a good deal more than he is.

response.text: At the first turn of the Hollis stairs, out of sight of the lobby, she’s waiting. She kisses him quick, easy as Sunday, and says against his mouth, “Morning, Youngstown,” and is up the last flight before he has his eyes open.
response.else: At the first turn of the Hollis stairs, out of sight of the lobby, she’s waiting. She kisses him quick, and it surprises them both, and she says against his mouth, “Morning, Youngstown,” and is up the last flight before he has his eyes open.

response: The pencil in her hair has left a small sore place at his temple from the way in. He is fairly sure she meant that too.
Caleb Hargrove comes round the turn below with his arms full of Hume, and sees nothing whatsoever, loudly, all the way up past him.

s03.slug: MONDAY · 1:05 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — THE LAW WITHOUT A LAWGIVER
body: Somebody has won the war with the radiator under 302’s middle window, and for the first time since January the room is warm: the sophomores have their coats hung off the backs of their chairs and the windows have fogged at the corners. Jack at the door end under the clock, Lena at the window end. Caleb beside Jack, both knees going under the table. Yusuf beside Caleb with his head on his arms. Evan Marsh at the door with the roster on its clipboard and no pen in his hand yet.
Hale comes in with *The Moviegoer* and drops it on the oak from a height. “We decided nothing,” he says. “Percy would be delighted.”

body.text: For the first ten minutes he doesn’t look at the door end of the table at all.
On his way past the clock: “Mr. Costigan. Still unbecoming?”
On his way past the clock: “Mr. Costigan, who believes in A paragraphs.”

body: “Business. Thursday week is the Marisol Forum, at which the university pays to watch two people disagree in front of a pitcher of water. This year’s motion is *That one can be good without God*. I am proposing it.” He takes his chair. “And Miss Broussard has volunteered to lose to me in public.”
“Volunteered,” Lena says from the window end, and leaves it there.

“Hence Anscombe.” He holds up Thursday’s photocopy by one corner, “Modern Moral Philosophy,” a stapled sheaf gone furry at the staple. “Elizabeth Anscombe. A Catholic woman who smoked, had seven children, and frightened my supervisor. Nineteen fifty-eight, and my profession hasn’t had a quiet night since. She is the best thing Miss Broussard has, and Miss Broussard knows it.” He lays it down. “I’ve heard my own arguments. I should like, just this once, to hear them from the outside. So I shan’t argue with Miss Broussard today. Mr. Costigan will be me. He’s been rehearsing since October.”

Beside Jack, Caleb turns with the face of a Central Valley boy watching his two favorite wrestlers agree to a steel cage. Down the table Yusuf lifts his head off his arms. “Can I be Mr. Costigan, then?” Hale doesn’t dignify it, and the head goes back down.
At the window end Lena pushes her sleeves up to the elbow — Jack has seen that before; somebody is about to have a bad afternoon — and gets up out of her chair to say it standing.

“I’ll give the motion its best day,” she says. “A man without God can be brave. He can be kind, and honest, and keep his word, and I’ve met him, and so has everybody at this table. Saint Paul met him. Romans two: the law written on their hearts, their conscience bearing witness. I am not going to stand up at the Forum and tell a good atheist he isn’t good. He is.”

She takes the pencil out of her hair. Her hair comes down on that side and she doesn’t notice. “But that isn’t what the motion means by *good*. In that room *good* means *ought*. You ought to keep a promise. You ought not to lie. And Anscombe’s point — half a century on and still sitting there — is that *ought*, said that way, with that thunder on it, is a word left over from a law. God’s law. Take away the lawgiver and the word goes on standing there, frowning, after everybody’s gone home. It’s like *criminal*, after somebody abolished criminal law. You can still call a man a criminal. You just can’t tell me what court.”
She sits, and looks up the oak at him, and waits. Caleb’s knees stop.

Jack has read the Anscombe twice — once on his break at the Anchor with the Hobart going and a wet thumb, once this morning on the Hollis steps waiting for eleven — and he knows what Hale would say back. Knowing it and saying it in Hale’s voice are two different jobs.

choices.text: *Euthyphro: if God commands it because it’s good, you don’t need the command; if it’s good because he commands it, it’s arbitrary.*
response: He sits back the way Hale sits back, arms folded, chin down, and gives it to her in the best Oxford he owns. Underneath, where Hale keeps his Yorkshire, Jack’s Yorkshire is terrible, and the table is kind enough not to say so yet.

“Plato had this sorted before your Church had a roof, Miss Broussard. Either God commands the good because it *is* good — in which case the good was there first, He’s only passing it along, and the atheist can go straight to it — or it’s good because He says so, in which case it’s whim, and you’re asking us to bow to a mood. Pick a horn.”
At the window end Lena’s chin comes up.

choices.text: *Take Anscombe’s own advice: drop “ought.” Aristotle called a coward a coward without a lawgiver.*
response: “Then let us take Professor Anscombe’s advice,” he says, in Hale. “Drop *ought*. She tells us to, if we can manage it, and do ethics the way Aristotle did. Very well. Aristotle called a coward a coward and a just man just without a lawgiver anywhere in the building. He didn’t need *ought* to see a man run from the line. Neither do you.”
Lena looks at him down the oak a moment longer than she needs to, and doesn’t write anything down.

choices.text: “Professor Anscombe would have taken my side out of contrariness.”
response: “Professor Anscombe,” Jack says, down his nose, the full length of the oak, “would have taken my side out of contrariness.”
The table laughs, Caleb loudest. Lena gives him nothing at all, down the whole length of the oak, and he can see what it costs her.

choices.text: “She’s right that the word’s gone strange. I hear it at the Anchor — ‘You *ought* to.’ Never who to.”
response: “She’s right that the word’s gone strange,” he says, and forgets for a minute to be Hale. “I hear it at the Anchor. Some guy at the counter, to his kid with the pancakes: ‘You *ought* to eat that.’ Never who to.”
At the window end Lena smiles at her pad.

body.text: “Euthyphro,” Lena says, to Hale, not to him. “He went straight to Euthyphro. Professor, he’s been rehearsing since *Plato*.”
“He’s taking Anscombe’s advice against Anscombe,” Lena says, to Hale, not to him. “That isn’t argument, that’s identity theft.”
“She would have taken my side, Professor,” Lena says, to Hale, not to him, “and then argued with me about it the whole way home.”
“He conceded in the first round,” Lena says, to Hale, not to him. “He’s playing you very badly, Professor, and I intend to let him.”

body: The Anscombe lies open in front of her, and she doesn’t look at it. “So. Fine. Drop *ought*, the way she says, and keep the virtues. Courage, justice, temperance, prudence — Aristotle’s kitchen, every jar on the shelf where he left it.” She holds up the pencil. “But his virtues are *for* something. A good knife cuts. A good eye sees. A good man does — what? Whatever a man is *for*. That’s the function argument, book one, and the house stands on it. My Mémère’s black iron pot is for a roux. She never had to ask what it meant. The man who poured it in a foundry in Birmingham meant it.” She leans in over the oak. “And *function* is a word that means somebody meant something. Saint Thomas walks straight through that door — the fifth way, the arrow and the archer. If a thing is *for* something, somebody’s aiming it.”
At the door, Evan clicks his pen.
From halfway down the side, mildly, Hale: “She’s brought the Angelic Doctor to a fistfight, Mr. Costigan. Do try to keep up.”

Jack thinks of Frank’s garage on Glenwood: the pegboard, with the outline of every tool drawn round it in marker so you’d know what was missing, and on every one of them, somewhere, a maker’s name stamped into the steel. Craftsman. Snap-on. Somebody meant every one. He is supposed to be arguing the other side, and the garage is no help to him at all.
“A knife cuts,” Jack says, “and nobody has to — ”
“ — bless the knife, no. But somebody forged it.”
“Or it’s just a rock that — ”
“ — happened to be sharp? Then you mean *lucky*. And you can’t owe luck a thing. Luck doesn’t keep books.”

Her hair is down on the one side where the pencil was, and her medal has swung forward and lies on the oak at the end of its chain, and the pencil is pointed up the length of the table at him, and the room is warm, and Jack, who is supposed to be an atheist from Yorkshire by way of Oxford, has to look down at Hale’s photocopy for a second to remember which side he’s on. He knows what Hale would do with the archer, because he has watched Hale do it since October: decline the ground she’s picked, and go round it, to something with fur.

choices.text: *Foot: a wolf that won’t hunt with the pack is a defective wolf. No one had to mean the wolf.*
response: “Philippa Foot,” he says, giving it every syllable, as Hale does a name he respects. “The wolf that eats the kill and won’t hunt with the pack. He’s *defective*, Miss Broussard: a bad wolf, as a root that won’t take up water is a bad root. The wolf’s own life sets the standard. You want a someone behind every *for*. Foot gives you a *for* with no one behind it, and it still tells the wolf when he’s failed. No one had to mean the wolf.”
Lena opens her mouth, and shuts it, and writes FOOT across the top of her pad.

choices.text: *Darwin wrote the function in. No one signed it.*
response: “Darwin wrote the function in,” he says. “A few million years of wolves that hunted and ate, and wolves that didn’t and starved. The purpose is in there, Miss Broussard, right enough. It just hasn’t got a signature on it. Ask the wolves who didn’t. Oh — you can’t. That’s rather the point.”
He says it in Hale’s dry, finished way, every consonant paid for, and sits there with the sound of it in the room and doesn’t hate it.

choices.text: “My dishwasher has a function. The Hobart’s never once asked who meant it.”
response: “My dishwasher has a function,” Jack says. “The Hobart’s never once asked who meant it. It does four hundred plates a night and hasn’t got a theory of itself to its name.”
Lena laughs. She puts her head back and laughs up at the ceiling of Hale’s seminar room and lets it go as far as it wants.

choices.text: “A wolf doesn’t feel guilty. That’s your best point, and I’m supposed to be Hale.”
response: “A wolf doesn’t feel guilty,” he says, and isn’t Hale at all for the length of it. “That’s your best point, and I’m supposed to be Hale. It doesn’t lie awake. It isn’t sorry. Whatever the wolf has, it isn’t a conscience.”
On her pad she draws one clean line through something she’d written. She won’t need it now.

s03b.slug: MONDAY · 1:45 PM · HOLLIS 302 — WHAT WE OWE

body.text: “Fine. A defective wolf. Nobody had to mean the wolf.”
“I believe him about the Hobart,” Lena says, to Hale.
“He’s supposed to be you, Professor, and he’s agreeing with me twice. I’d mark that down, if I were you.”
“He’s supposed to be you, Professor, and he’s agreeing with me. I’d mark that down, if I were you.”

body: Caleb has stopped writing altogether. He sits with the green pen in his fist like a sparkler on the Fourth, turning from one end of the oak to the other, and when Lena draws herself up to go again he says “*Yes*,” into his fist, and doesn’t seem to know he’s said it.
Lena turns the Anscombe face down on the oak. She has it by heart, or near enough, and whatever she has left isn’t in it.

“But leave the wolf in the woods,” Lena says. “Come inside. You borrow your neighbor’s truck. You back it into a post at the Winn-Dixie and put a dent in the tailgate the size of a fist, and you bring it home and park it nose-out so he won’t see, and he never does. Now. How do you feel?”
Jack can see the post. He can see the dent, and Frank’s face, and the driveway on Glenwood.

“Not *defective*,” she says. “You don’t sit there feeling like a wolf with a bad leg. You feel like you *owe*. Every language I’ve got says it the same way — I owe him, I owe her, *je te dois*. And he’ll never find out, and you’ll owe him anyway, every time you see that truck in his driveway, till one of you dies. Owing is a debt, and a debt isn’t owed to the universe, or the species, or the pack. A debt is to a person.”
She has stopped looking at Hale. She’s looking up the length of the oak to the clock end, at him, and her pencil has stopped where it was.
“So take your lawgiver away,” she says. “Then tell me who it is you owe.”

The room goes quiet in a way it doesn’t go for arguments. Jack’s right hand is on the oak, and he doesn’t remember putting it there; under his palm the varnish is worn through to the wood, where forty years of elbows have been. He has three of Hale’s answers, good ones. He picks one up.

choices.text: *Scanlon: we owe it to each other. The whole book. There’s no God in it.*
choices.key: Playing Hale against Lena in his seminar, you told her we owe it to each other, and there’s no God in the sentence.
response: “Scanlon,” he says, and Hale’s voice comes back onto him like a coat off a hook. “*What We Owe to Each Other.* The book is your answer, Miss Broussard, and he put it in the title so nobody could miss it. We owe it to each other. What I could justify to you; what you couldn’t reasonably reject. Not a soul up a mountain with tablets. Just the man whose truck you dented, and what he could fairly ask of you. The creditor is sitting across the table. There’s no God in the sentence.”
Lena says, “Hm,” which from her is a door left open.

choices.text: *“Owing” is a market word. Hale would say the market isn’t sacred either.*
choices.key: Playing Hale against Lena, you told her owing is a market word, and the market isn’t sacred either.
response: “*Owing*.” He holds the word up by its tail, as Hale holds up a student’s favorite adjective. “That’s the counting-house, Miss Broussard. Debts, creditors, accounts settled. You’ve borrowed the market’s language to sneak a creditor into the room, and I’d remind you the market isn’t sacred either.” And in his own voice, because he can’t help it: “Ask anybody in Youngstown.”
Halfway down the side of the table Hale hums, very low: a man hearing his own argument come out of somebody else’s mouth and liking the tune.

choices.text: “It does feel like owing somebody who isn’t in the room.”
choices.key: Playing Hale against Lena, you admitted it feels like owing somebody who isn’t in the room.
response: “It does feel like owing somebody who isn’t in the room,” Jack says, with no Oxford on it anywhere. He is thinking about the tailgate, and a post at a Winn-Dixie he has never seen and could draw.
The room is quiet a second. Lena doesn’t press the advantage. She looks at him down the oak, and then down at her pad.

choices.text: “Newman made that argument in 1870, and it’s been in the infirmary ever since.”

I grant you the wolf. Then the wolf can be damaged. He can’t be *wronged*. The man with the truck can, and that difference is the whole Forum. *Ought* has been living off an inheritance it won’t name.” The wolf was his. What she has built on top of it is all hers. I grant you him. He’s real and I owe him. My point is he was never the only one at the table, and *ought* has been living off an inheritance it won’t name.” The creditor was his. The inheritance is all hers. She picks the pencil back up and points it at him the length of the oak. “I’m using that Thursday week. With attribution, Professor Costigan.”

Lena sits back in her chair and looks up the oak at him, delighted, and makes no effort at all to hide it. “He *gave* it to me,” she tells the table. “He was supposed to be you, Professor, and he sat in that chair and gave me my case.” Hale takes his time looking down the table at the door end. “You’ve given her the Forum, Mr. Costigan. I shall have to find another me.”

Hale lets the room settle. He leans forward on his forearms. “And what does Miss Broussard say to the good atheist in the third row,” he asks, “who will be real, and will be listening?” Lena opens her mouth, and closes it. At the other end of the oak Jack has the beginning of an answer and no idea whose side it’s on. Both of them sit with it.

body: Hale closes *The Moviegoer* on his thumb, and the chairs start going back, and over the sophomores getting into their coats he says, “Miss Broussard, stay. Mr. Costigan — you make a very passable me. It’s unnerving. Go away.”

Jack goes away. At the window end Lena, still in her chair, watches him go with her chin on her fist, and Hale is already pulling his own chair round to face her. The door has nearly shut behind Jack when Hale’s voice comes through the gap, already going: “Now. Your opening is a third too long, and you know which third —”

The Hollis steps still have the sun on them. The coffee crowd has gone in, and somewhere around the side of the building a skateboard goes back and forth over the same crack. Jack takes the top step again, out of the traffic, and gives it twenty minutes. He’d give it longer. The Bic on the back of his hand has worn down to a blue smear in which, if you knew, you could still make out a seven. Saturday is five days off. He has a reservation, a hundred and sixty-two dollars and no jacket, and it turns out the list frightens him a good deal less than the word *occasion* did.
At twenty to three she comes out with three pages of Hale’s fountain pen in her fist, the tall hand that leans backward, and sits down beside him without a word, and holds the fist up.
“He gave me his notes.” She opens her hand. “On *himself*. He wants me to win. He’d rather die than say it.”
“Are you going to?”
She folds the three pages once down the middle, and puts them inside her jean jacket, and turns her face up into the sun with her eyes shut.
“Win? Lord, yes.” And then, with her eyes still shut: “Seven-thirty. I don’t know a thing about it.”
Jack leans back on his elbows on the warm step and doesn’t say a thing about it either.

Dr. Fenner has drawn a beach on the board: a long flat line, and the surf as a row of little humps along it with one gap in the row. Out through the gap he chalks an arrow, skinny at the bottom and fanned at the top, a tree with no trunk to speak of. “Rip current,” he says, turning round, pleased with it. “Not a rip *tide*. If I see rip *tide* on a midterm I will weep in front of you.” He taps along the shore. “Feeder.” The gap. “Neck.” The fan, out past the break. “Head.” All the water the waves pile up on a beach has to get back out somehow, he says, and it finds the low place and goes out through it all at once, fast, faster in a good one than anybody in this room can swim.

“It doesn’t pull you under. Everybody thinks it pulls you under. It takes you out past the break and lets go of you there.” He points the chalk up the tiers. “The people who drown in one drown swimming at the beach. They can see exactly where they want to be, and they go straight at it with everything they’ve got, and it’s stronger than everything they’ve got. Don’t fight it. Swim parallel. Along the shore, out of the neck — most of them aren’t thirty yards wide. Then swim in.”

One of the surfers in the fourth row says you can also just ride it out to the lineup, it’s a free ride, and Fenner aims the chalk at him with real joy. “That young man has a *board*. That young man is not the population I’m worried about.”

s04a.slug: TUESDAY · 12:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY — NOT A DRESS
body: Delgado’s lobby at lunch is the wall of mailboxes, little brass doors with combination dials, and the front desk with a sophomore behind it eating a Commons wrap over *Organic Chemistry*, and the Yellow Pages back on its shelf under the bulletin board where he put it yesterday. Jack is spinning his combination for nothing — a Residential Life flyer about the dryers, two-for-one from Giorgio’s — when Laney Price comes in from the mail window with a box.

It’s a USPS Express Mail box, white with the blue eagle, and she has it hugged to her front with both arms, contraband. The label is in a careful upright hand, every letter standing on its own two feet — *Magdalena Broussard, Delgado Hall 217* — and up in the corner, the return address: *N. Dupre St., New Orleans, LA.*

“This is *not* a dress,” Laney says, before he has opened his mouth. “It is *books*. Heavy Catholic books. Her mama is sending her Lent reading. Encyclicals.” She hugs the box tighter. It weighs, by the look of it, about as much as a sweater.
It isn’t Lena’s hand. Lena’s leans forward like it’s late for something.
Laney shifts the box onto one hip. Her face comes up like a stadium at dusk, bank by bank, and she fills up for it, and he can see Saturday rising in her, with advice in it.
“Don’t,” Jack says.
Laney shuts her mouth on it. She looks at him over the box, wounded to the soul and thrilled about it.
“I was *only*,” she says, “going to say wear socks that match. On Sunday in the lounge you had on one navy and one black, fireman, and I said nothing, because it was the Lord’s day.”
“They’ll match.”

“They had *better*. I have seen your closet, Jack Costigan. Theodore gave me the tour. I had to sit down.” She hoists the box higher. “And Saturday from six o’clock, she is *mine*. You don’t call, you don’t come down, you don’t stand on that landing with your face. You will be *received*, at the time appointed, like a gentleman, and not one minute before. And if you so much as shake this, I will Express Mail *you* back to Ohio. In pieces. Overnight. Insured.”
She’s still going — something about a lint roller, and a girl in Highland Park who wore white to a cotillion and has never been seen again — when the RAZR goes off in his pocket, twice.

s05m.slug: TUESDAY · 7:00 PM · THE UCEN, UPSTAIRS — THE TIDE
body: The *Marisol Tide* lives up a flight of stairs from the UCen’s Panda Express, behind a door with a red Dymo label on it, under a fluorescent tube that makes everybody in the room look recently exhumed. It’s a long room with a layout table down the middle and proofs pinned to a corkboard in overlapping ranks, back issues in drifts against the wall, and in the corner the dead iMac G4 still holding the AP Stylebook open on its neck like a lectern. The radiator under the window is on full and hissing to itself.

Margot is at the end of the layout table with her notebook open and the Nokia face down at her elbow, in a black turtleneck, the only person Jack knows who can look like the front page of a French newspaper with orange chicken coming up the stairs.
“Sit,” she says. “You’re the Catholic.”
“I’m *a* Catholic.”

“You’re the useful one. The rest of Newman is either in the choir or on a retreat about it.” She turns a page. “April twenty-sixth is fifty-five days from tonight. One year since Nora Calloway went off the Point.” She says the name without any ceremony at all. “The *Tide* would like three hundred words. Candles. A quote from somebody at the vigil. A photograph of the cross with flowers on it. Page six, under the ad for the tanning place.” She sets the pen down. “I intend to write four thousand words of what happened to her.”
“What happened to her was in the paper.”

She reaches into the drift of back issues by her chair and comes up with last April’s, and lays it on the table: a photograph of candles along a low wall at night, and a smaller one of a girl in a choir robe with her hair pinned up, laughing at whoever held the camera. “Two hundred and eleven words,” Margot says. “I counted. Forty of them are the police.”

“That was a sentence in the paper. *Accidental fall.* A girl sits on the wrong side of a wall at night, and the police say *accident* in about the time it takes to say *accident*, and everyone is very relieved, and not one person asks what a sophomore who sang in the Newman choir was doing on that wall at midnight by herself.” She looks at him, level. “A sentence isn’t a story. She was a person. Somebody should find out which one.”
“Her family might want the candles,” Jack says.

“Her family can have the candles. Candles are for the family.” Margot taps the photograph of the wall. “The paper is for the rest of us, who walked past that cross all year on the way to the beach and never asked whose it was.”
It’s a good reason. He’d like it to be a worse one.

“I need Father Osei,” Margot says. “He said her memorial Mass. He knew her the way a priest knows people, which is the one way I don’t have.” “I need a Catholic who can get me a priest who won’t hide behind a collar.”
“He doesn’t hide behind it. He just wears it.”
“Then he won’t mind being asked.”
“I’ll tell him you want to talk to him,” Jack says. “That’s not the same as him talking.”

“It never is.” She turns the notebook round on the table and slides it across to him. In her small hard print there is a list headed *In Memory of Nora Calloway — FB group*, a handful of names, and a box drawn round three of them. *Julian.* *Priya.* *Magdalena Broussard.*
“Julian sang with her,” Margot says. “Priya I can work out. And I would like to know why a freshman who never met her is in a memorial group.”

Jack knows why. At All Souls, in front of the Book of the Dead, Lena wrote Nora Calloway’s name under her grandmother’s, and when she saw him see it she said Nora had been her host at Preview Weekend, last April. It isn’t his to give Margot.
Margot waits. She is extremely good at waiting.

s05t.slug: TUESDAY · 7:00 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — DINNER SCHOOL
body: 412 has been converted. The two desks are pushed end to end down the middle of the room under a white Delgado bath towel for a tablecloth, the desk lamp is turned to the wall for candlelight, and over Jack’s bed the crucifix presides. Theo is in shirtsleeves with the cuffs turned back twice and a dish towel over his forearm, humming something of Sinatra’s, low, a little behind the band, the way the man himself did it.

At Jack’s end there is a place setting that must have come out of the Commons in installments over most of a week: a dinner plate with the Anacapa crest, a bread plate, a water glass, a juice glass promoted to wine, a knife, a spoon, and three forks. Two are Commons forks. The third is white plastic.
“For verisimilitude,” Theo says. “There is always a fork you have never seen before in your life. You will not know what it’s for. It will be looking at you. Sit.”
Jack sits. Theo whips the napkin off the plate — a Commons napkin, paper, folded up into something with ambitions — and holds it up by one corner.

“The Bishop’s Mitre, Costigan. Appropriately. And it goes in your lap before the bread. Before the *bread*. You don’t tuck it in your collar, you are not eating a lobster on a pier in Maine. You don’t snap it open like a bedsheet. It simply arrives on your knee. It was always there.”

He taps the forks down the row with the butter knife like a xylophone. “Outside in. Salad, fish, meat. A slow push in toward the plate, one course at a time. Kubrick would have shot it in a hundred and twelve takes and fired the waiter.”
“And the plastic one?”
“The plastic one is the one you don’t know. When in doubt, watch her. She was raised by people who own a gravy boat.”

He produces the wine list: another napkin, unfolded, in Theo’s own looping hand, a dozen lines of French, most of which, when Jack reads it, is *Point Break*. *Château Bodhi ’91. Cuvée Johnny Utah, blanc. Les Ex-Présidents, réserve.*

“You’re eighteen,” Theo says. “In California. In a room with tablecloths. They will hand you the list anyway, because they are professionals and you will be wearing a jacket. You open it. You read it. You hand it back as if you’ve read it and found it wanting. And you say, ‘We’ll start with water.’ You never say *tap*.”
Jack opens the napkin, reads *Les Ex-Présidents*, and hands it back.
“No. You handed that back like a parking ticket. Again. With contempt. *Gentle* contempt. You’ve had better.”
He does it again. Theo shuts his eyes.
“Better. Truffaut would have kept that one.”

“The tip.” Theo pulls out the desk chair across from him and sits, for the first time all night. “You tip like a man who has washed dishes. Which is to say obscenely. You know what the night looks like from the back of the house. Behave accordingly.”
He reaches out and lines the plastic fork up with the other two, and keeps his eyes on it.

“My father took me to places like that when he had something to tell me,” he says. “He liked a room with a man in a white jacket two tables off who wouldn’t blink.” He moves the fork a hair to the left. “That’s what tablecloths are for. Witnesses with manners.”

Then he’s up again, flicking the towel at a Commons dinner roll on the bread plate, and the moment has gone wherever Theo sends them. “Bread. You *tear* it. You never cut it. You tear off a bite, and you butter the bite. You are not spackling a wall.”

They do bread. They do the soup spoon, away from you, and the salt, which is passed with the pepper because they are married. They do what to do with your hands, which is nothing, beautifully. By a quarter to ten he is sliding the three forks back into the pocket of his coat to be returned to the Commons the way they came, a little at a time, and he says, with his back to Jack, “Take the navy.”

s06g.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:30 PM · THE ANCHOR — RUDY’S WEDDING
body: Half past four on a Wednesday is the Anchor’s dead hour, between the late lunches and the fishermen’s supper, when the place belongs to the pie case and the ceiling fans. Merle’s stool is empty. Rudy’s radio sits dark on its shelf over the grill. Gloria is at the end of the counter with the paper folded to the crossword and a grease pencil stuck through the knot of her hair, and she looks up when the bell goes over the door, and back down.
“Hon.”
“Gloria. I need a jacket.” And because she waits, he gives her the rest in a sentence: Saturday, the place at the end of the wharf, a jacket, and him with a Carhartt.
She fills in a word. She keeps her eyes on the next clue and says something in Spanish over her shoulder toward the kitchen, quick and flat, and the only part of it Jack catches is *Rudy*.

Rudy comes out of the back drying his hands, hears her out, and looks at Jack — at the shoulders, the length of the arms, a cook sizing a cut of meat — and goes on out the back door to the lot without a word. Gloria does two more clues. Jack stands at the counter where he has stood since September, on the wrong side of it, with his hands in his pockets.

The back door bangs. Rudy comes in with a dry-cleaning bag over his arm, the plastic gone cloudy with age and a paper tag stapled at the neck. He hangs it on the hook by the register and peels the plastic up.

It’s brown. Not a little brown: brown with conviction, a chocolate brown with wide lapels and a sheen to it, and when the plastic lifts a little sweet cologne comes out of the lining, faint, from a long time ago.
“My wedding,” Rudy says. “My mother picked it out. Penney’s, in Oxnard. She said brown doesn’t show anything.” He looks at it, and at Jack, and at it again, apologetic. “Mijo. It’s brown.”
“Brown is a color,” Gloria says, from the crossword.

It’s a size too big. The shoulders sit out past his own like a porch roof, and the sleeves come down over his knuckles. Gloria comes round the end of the counter with the tin from under the register — an old Danish butter cookie tin like the one Nonna keeps buttons in, full of buttons and safety pins and straight pins — and puts a row of pins between her lips, and takes his wrist and turns his arm out, and folds the sleeve up two inches and pins it, and the other one, fast, the way she does a lattice.
She stands back and looks at the shoulders. “You’ll grow.”
“I’m done growing, Gloria.”
“Not there.” She tips her chin at his back, at the Hobart’s work on it. “Saturday morning. I’ll hem it. Nine o’clock.”

response: “I’ll bring it back better than I found it.”
“Bring it back, mijo,” Rudy says. “That’s enough.”
Gloria takes a pin out of her mouth to say “Hm,” and puts it back.

response: “Did you dance in this?”
“All night,” Rudy says.
“He stepped on my sister,” Gloria says, round the pins.
Rudy, already on his way back to the grill: “*Once*.”

response: “I can pay you.”
Gloria looks at him over the sleeve. “You can wash dishes in it.”
She goes back round the counter to her crossword, and it is a full minute, standing there with his arms pinned, before Jack works out that she was joking.

s06t.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — THE NAVY
body: “Theo. Can I borrow the navy?”

Theo is at his desk with the laptop open on something in black and white. He closes it. He gets up and crosses to his closet and runs a hand along the row and takes it out by the hanger, already the right one.

It’s his best. Navy wool so soft it’s barely there, no padding in the shoulders, a lining Jack would have to call *plum* if anybody made him, and inside the collar a label in Italian that Jack can’t pronounce and isn’t going to try in front of Theo.

Theo holds it open behind him like a bullfighter’s cape. Jack puts his arms in. It goes on and settles, and in the mirror on the back of the closet door there’s somebody Jack doesn’t know — somebody out of a movie about a better school. It fits at the collar. It fits at the wrists. It fits everywhere except across the back, where it was cut for a man who has never lifted anything heavier than a Criterion box set, and Jack has been racking mugs at the Anchor since September.
Theo pinches the seam across his shoulder blades between thumb and finger, and tests it.
“Don’t reach for anything.”
“What if she drops something?”
“Let it lie. She’ll think you have depths.”

Theo walks round him slowly, a director walking a set he isn’t sure of. “Shoulders back. No — *back*, not *up*. You’re not bracing for a punch, you’re a man with a reservation. You button it standing and unbutton it when you sit. Never the bottom button. The bottom button is for Midwesterners and the dead.”
“I’m a Midwesterner.”
“Not on Saturday.”

He takes a white pocket square from a drawer and holds it up against the breast pocket, and looks, and puts it away again. “No. You’d fidget with it. She’d watch you fidget with it, and know everything.”

He works round Jack with pins out of a hotel sewing kit he has clearly never opened for himself, tugging a cuff, turning the collar up and down again, stepping back, coming in. Whatever this is for Theo, he’s good at it, and his face says he likes being asked. Jack catches his eye in the mirror and grins. “Don’t grin in it,” Theo says. “It’ll get ideas, and I’ll never get it back.”

choices.text: “It’s the best thing I’ve ever had on.”
response: “It’s the best thing I’ve ever had on.”
“It’s the best thing *I’ve* ever had on,” Theo says, “and it’s never looked like that.”
He takes Jack by both shoulders and turns him to face the mirror, and walks off across the room to the window, so that what his face is doing is the window’s business.

choices.text: “Do I have to give it back if she says yes?”
response: “Do I have to give it back if she says yes?”
“She’s *said* yes,” Theo says. “You have to give it back either way.”
He goes back to his desk and opens the laptop on the black-and-white picture again, a man for whom the matter is closed.

choices.text: *Stand still and let him pin it.*
response: Jack stands still with his arms held a little out from his sides, posed for a tailor out of some old movie, and lets him.
Theo comes round the front with a pin between his teeth and looks, and goes on looking, and doesn’t put it anywhere. There’s nowhere to put it. He takes the pin out of his mouth.
“Arms *down*, Costigan.”

s06v.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:20 PM · MISSION STREET, ST. VINCENT DE PAUL — WALTER
body: The St. Vincent de Paul on Mission Street has a bell on the door and the smell they all have, old wool and mothballs and somebody’s attic, and Jack is home the minute it reaches him. Ma bought his Confirmation shoes at the one on the South Side, black, a size big to grow into, and he grew into them.

The men’s jackets hang on a rack by the window in a long patient row: a powder-blue tuxedo jacket with a ruffle still pinned to it, somebody’s high-school letterman, a corduroy with elbow patches that has sat through years of faculty meetings, a black blazer gone green across the shoulders. And at the end of the row, a brown herringbone sport coat, heavy and plain and well made, with the price on a tag on a safety pin. *$9.*

He puts it on. It fits across the back as if the man who wore it carried things for a living too. In the long mirror by the dressing room it makes him look older, or like somebody’s uncle at a wedding, and either one will do.
There’s something stiff in the breast pocket. He takes it out.

body.text: In Loving Memory · Walter J. Pruszynski · 1921–2009 · St. Joseph the Worker · Lord, make me an instrument of your peace.

body: On the front, St. Francis, with a bird on his finger.

At the register a small woman in a green cardigan is pricing a box of paperbacks with a sticker gun. She has the look Jack grew up around at St. Brigid’s: white hair cut short, good flat shoes, a plain silver cross, a sister out of her habit since the seventies and never out of the job. She sees the card in his hand.
“The family brought in all his suits,” she says. “In the fall. After the funeral.”

*Walter J. Pruszynski.* A boy in the Depression, then, and old enough for the war. It’s a name off the mailboxes on the East Side at home, off the St. Stanislaus bulletin, off the honor roll in the vestibule at St. Brigid’s with the little gold stars by it.
“Walter,” Jack says.

She comes round from behind the counter and turns his collar down at the back, where it has folded under, without asking, with the hand of a woman who has done it for a great many boys. “St. Joe’s,” she says. “The Worker. Out on the Westside. Every Sunday of his life, the eight o’clock.” She clicks a sticker onto a Reader’s Digest Condensed Book. “You’re taking it?”

choices.text: *Keep the card in the pocket. Say one for Walter.*
response: He puts the card back in the breast pocket where Walter, or whoever loved Walter, left it, and lays a five and four ones from the Anchor envelope on the glass. While she rings it up he says it, low, to the glass. “Eternal rest grant unto him, O Lord —”
“— and let perpetual light shine upon him,” she says along with him, counting into the drawer, as easily as the price of the jacket. “May he rest in peace.”
“Amen.”
She pats the back of his hand on the glass, twice, and goes back to her paperbacks.

choices.text: *Hand the card back — it’s the family’s.*
response: He holds the card out to her across the counter. “This should go back to the family.”

She won’t take it. She keeps both hands on the sticker gun and shakes her head. “They gave them all away. Every suit he had.” She looks at the coat on him, at the shoulders, and nods at it. “He’d want it worn.”
Jack puts the card back in the breast pocket himself, behind the flap, where it was.

choices.text: “Walter, you and me are going to dinner.”
response: “Walter,” he tells the coat, “you and me are going to dinner.”
The woman looks up from the paperbacks, surprised into a smile. “Oh, he’d have liked that. I’d bet you anything he danced at every wedding at St. Joe’s.”
Out on Mission Street the wind is coming up off the harbor, and in Walter’s coat Jack is warm.

s07.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — THE FLOOR IS YOURS
body: Somewhere on three a shower is running. Otherwise the building has gone to its Wednesday quiet, all its doors shut on reading, and the tube over the landing between two and three is doing its best, dim at the end where it has been dim since October.

Lena is on her step under it with her knees up and a yellow legal pad on them, and on top of the pad, face down, three pages of Hale: the fountain-pen hand showing backward through the sheets, tall and leaning back, nothing Jack can read. She’s in sweatpants and a Saints sweatshirt with the sleeves shoved to the elbow. His black Bic is behind her ear.
Where the pad sticks out from under them he can see her own hand, slanting, crossed out and written over, arrows up the margin, a word boxed so hard the pen has gone through.

“He gave me three pages on how to beat him,” she says, when he is still on the last stair, “and he’s wrong about two of them, and I can’t tell which two. You’re Hale. Stand there. He doesn’t sit for this. He walks, and he puts his hands behind his back like the Duke of Edinburgh.”
He stands on the landing and puts his hands behind his back and lifts his chin at the fire extinguisher. He has watched the man do it for two semesters.
“Miss Broussard,” he says, in Hale. “The floor is yours. Do try not to bleed on it.”
“Your Yorkshire’s from Pittsburgh.”
He drops Hale entirely. “Take that back.”
“It says *yinz*. Hush. You’re Hale. Hale doesn’t argue with women on staircases. He lets them finish, and then he ruins them.”
She stands up for it — on her step, so she has the height on him — and lets the pad hang at her side and doesn’t look at it once.

“I grant the motion its best man,” she says. “Y’all have met him. He sits up three nights running with his mother in the hospital and never says grace over the vending-machine coffee. He has never once asked God for a thing.” She lets that stand a moment, and then, out of the speech, quick: “Paul, Romans, the law on their hearts — you heard that part Monday. I’m skipping it tonight.” And back in: “The Church has never said that man isn’t good. I won’t stand up here and say it either.”
“How *terribly* generous of Rome,” Jack says, in Hale, rocking on his heels. “The atheist may be good, on condition that he’s secretly a Catholic. Do tell him. He’ll be thrilled.”

“Better,” she says. “Still Pittsburgh.” And goes straight on over him. “But the motion doesn’t say a man can *do* good without God. It says one can *be* good. And the minute you call him good — the minute you say he *ought* to sit up with his mother, that he’d be failing somebody if he went home to bed — you have used a word that means a debt.”
At *ought* his thumb finds the corner of the pack through the canvas of his breast pocket.

“Then he owes it to *her*,” Jack says, Hale again, because Hale would have it ready. “To his mother. To the nurse. To the man he gave his word to. A fellow called Scanlon wrote four hundred pages on what we owe to each other, Miss Broussard, and never needed a ghost to do the collecting.”

“Then tell me why he feels it most when she’s dead.” She doesn’t raise her voice; she drops it, and he has to lean in to get it. “His mother dies on the third night. He goes home. He owes her nothing anymore — your Mr. Scanlon would tell him so, kindly. And he sits on the edge of his bed in his clothes, and he still owes her, and he knows it, and there is no one left on earth to pay.”

“We kept the word after we buried the one it was owed to, and it goes right on working on us anyway — a collection agency for a bank that closed fifty years ago, still sending letters.” She takes the Bic from behind her ear and points it at the third row, where there is a fire door. “I am not here to tell the good man in the third row that he’s wicked. I believe in him. I’m here to ask him who it is he thinks he owes.”
She stops. Up on three the shower has quit at some point; he didn’t hear it go.

It’s good. It is better than good. He stands on the landing with Hale’s hands still clasped behind him and can’t think of one thing Hale could say to it that she hasn’t already picked up off the table and put in her pocket.
She sits back down on her step and writes something at the top of the pad he can’t read from where he is.

body.text: “And you,” she says to the pad. “Last week, in 302. A silence that’s a promise. I’m stealing it. Hale’s motion is a silence about who’s owed.”

body: “Where is Saturday?” she says, writing.
“Saturday.”
“That’s not a *where*, Costigan.”
“Wear something you can walk in.”
She looks up at that and narrows her eyes at him, and something in them says she is going through every place in Marisol a person could walk to, and coming up empty, and hating it.
He comes up the one step and leans down and kisses her.

The pad goes off her knee and down a stair with a slap. Her mouth is surprised for about half a second and then isn’t; it tastes of the Commons’ terrible cocoa; the back of his hand brushes the medal where it lies against her collarbone and it is cold, the only cold thing on the landing. It’s short. He straightens up, and would very much like to do it again, and she is looking at him from her step with the Bic still in her hand.
She leans down and gets the pad off the stair below, and smooths the top sheet flat on her knee, and sets the pen to it.
“Again,” she says. “From the top. And give me a note this time.”

choices.text: *Tell her the true note: she wins it in the first two minutes or not at all.*
choices.key: On her landing the night she rehearsed for the Forum, you told Lena she’d win it in the first two minutes or not at all.
response: “He decides in the first two minutes whether you’re worth his evening,” Jack says. “So does the room. You win it in the first two minutes or not at all. Start with the debt.”
She turns Hale’s first page over just far enough to write *2 MIN* along its top edge in capitals, and circles it, and circles it again.
“Goodnight, Youngstown.”
He goes up the stairs, and the last thing he hears before the fourth-floor door is her voice starting again from the top, low, to the wired glass.

choices.text: “Hale will try to make you say atheists are wicked. Don’t let him cast you.”
choices.key: On her landing the night she rehearsed for the Forum, you told Lena not to let Hale cast her as the woman who thinks atheists are wicked.
response: “He’ll try to make you say atheists are wicked,” Jack says. “That’s the play. He wants the woman in the movie who thinks the nice man’s going to hell. Don’t let him cast you.”
“He *would*,” she says, delighted and furious in the same face.
She throws the Bic at him. He gets it one-handed out of the air, and puts it in his pocket, and keeps it.

choices.text: “You’re better than him at this. Say it to his face.”
choices.key: On her landing the night she rehearsed for the Forum, you told Lena she was better than Hale at this, and to say it to his face.
response: “You’re better than him at this,” he says. “Say it to his face.”
“He told me to, once. It’s on a card in my missal at home.” She sets the pad down on the step beside her. “I intend to.”
She looks at him from her step and doesn’t say anything else, and it does for goodnight.

choices.text: *Listen to it a second time without a note.*
choices.key: On her landing the night she rehearsed for the Forum, you listened to her opening a second time without a note.
response: He doesn’t give her one. He puts his hands behind his back again, Hale’s hands, and waits.

She runs it from the top, and it’s better: she cuts a sentence he hadn’t noticed was weak, and slows down on *ought*, and leaves a silence after *who it is he thinks he owes* that he can feel on the back of his neck. At the end she stops and looks at him.
“That was the note,” she says.
She stays on her step and he stays on the landing, the pad on the stair between them, the stairwell quiet above and below.

s08.slug: THURSDAY · 10:58 AM · MORRO HALL 1100 — THE SEAT
body: Tuesday’s rain has all gone out to sea, and the bike racks outside Morro are jammed three deep and still filling, kickstands and chains and somebody’s U-lock dropped on the concrete, a hundred people locking up at once. Jack goes in with the crowd, up the side stairs into the noise of a hundred people finding their seats, and climbs to the back row under the exit sign.
Her desk is down.

She’s in it. She got here before him. Her own navy sweater with the cuffs pulled down over her hands, and the scarf, and her sunglasses pushed back into her hair to hold it off her face; a pen; her notebook open to a clean page with the date written at the top and nothing under it. Not his flannel.
She doesn’t look up at him. She doesn’t look anywhere else, either. She’s looking at the board, where Fenner is, where anybody in a lecture looks.

Nine days. For nine days he has told himself he wouldn’t know what to do if that desk came down, and it turns out what you do is sit. He sits. His own desk comes down with the same knock as every other desk in the room, and he gets out his notebook and his pen and puts his bag at his feet on his own side, and the seat she’s in is the same seat it has been since January.

body.text: The last time he was this close to her she was closing a screen door with both hands so it wouldn’t bang.
The last time he was this close to her she was at her porch rail with her back to him, and her shoulders went, and that was all he got.
The last time he was this close to her she was watching him go down her walk with her arms crossed tight and her mouth shut.
In the back of the notebook is a bookstore folder he bought yesterday for a dollar, because the spiral had started chewing the corners of what’s in it.
Down at the front, on the table by the door, Fenner’s wire tray for absentees sits where it always sits.

body: Fenner has the big roll-down map of the Pacific pulled over the board and is standing in front of it with a wooden pointer, happy as a man at a ballgame. “Last weekend’s,” he says, and touches the pointer to the coast of Chile, and then lays it flat across the blue in the middle of the map, as much of it as the pointer will cover. “Out here, in the deep water, a tsunami is about a foot high. A foot. And a hundred miles long, front to back. And it’s doing five hundred miles an hour, which is the plane most of you flew home on at Christmas.” He slides the pointer across the ocean toward them, slowly. “You could be out there on a boat eating a sandwich right on top of it. It goes under you. You don’t feel a thing.”

The pointer comes to the coastline and stops where the blue goes pale. “It’s when the bottom comes up,” Fenner says. “All that water has to go somewhere. That’s the only part of it anybody ever sees.”
Jack writes *a foot high* in his margin, and nothing after it. In January she would have leaned over and written something under it about the sandwich. Her pen stays on her own page.
Somebody down front asks whether it reached Santa Barbara. Fenner starts to answer, and looks up the tiers instead, pleased with something, and sees her.
“Ms. Callender. Welcome back. Your other half has been carrying the project.” He aims the pointer up at the two of them like a wand. “Pair 41, I’m putting you down for Tuesday. Both halves.”
Heads turn up the rows, a few. She nods at him once, eyes on her page, and goes on writing.
Of the last forty minutes Jack keeps nothing but the sound of her pen going along the page beside his.

At a quarter past twelve the room comes apart: desks slapping up all down the tiers, zippers, a hundred conversations starting at once and heading for the doors. She caps her pen and doesn’t get up. He opens the back of his notebook.

choices.text: *Hold out the folder — every one of hers.*
choices.key: When Skye came back to Oceanography, you held out the folder with all of her handouts and your notes across each.
response: He holds it out. It hangs there over the armrest with the room draining down the tiers past them, long enough for him to feel how stupid his arm looks, and then she takes it.
She opens it on her clean page.

choices.text: *Hold it out and say, “You missed three.”*
choices.key: When Skye came back to Oceanography, you held out her handouts and told her she’d missed three.
response: “You missed three,” he says, and holds it out.
She takes it without answering. Her thumb goes down the edge of the stack inside, counting it, while her eyes stay on the front of the room.

choices.text: *Set it on her desk and don’t say anything.*
choices.key: When Skye came back to Oceanography, you set her handouts on her desk and didn’t say anything.
response: He sets it on the corner of her desk and takes his hand back.
It sits there through a row of people squeezing past to the aisle. Then she draws it over to her with one finger.

choices.text: “Fenner’s tray has two with your name on them.”
choices.key: When Skye came back to Oceanography, you told her Fenner’s tray had two handouts with her name on them.
response: “Fenner’s tray has two with your name on them.”
She looks down the tiers at the wire basket on the table by the door, and doesn’t go and get them. She turns her capped pen end over end on the desk.

choices.text: “Skye.”
choices.key: When Skye came back to Oceanography, you said her name before anything else.
response: “Skye.”
He hasn’t said it since the bottom of her steps. Her pen stops turning. She turns her head and looks at him.

She doesn’t open anything. She sits with her hands on her clean page and looks at him while the row in front of them empties, a girl in a crew sweatshirt and two boys arguing about a quiz, down the row to the aisle and away.

body: “You don’t lie,” Skye says.
The room is going down the tiers past them in a slow loud tide of backpacks and coffee cups. He waits.

“I ran it back,” she says. “Tuesday. Every night since. I lie down and I run the whole porch, start to finish, like dailies. Every take. And I look for it, the place where you’re lying. I’m good at that.” Her eyes don’t leave his face. “I watched your hands. People lie with their hands; they never know where to put them. Yours just hung there, the entire time, like you’d forgotten you had any. And I watched you correct me about midnight. Do you know what a liar does when you get the time wrong? He lets you have it. Any time you want. You stood on my porch in the middle of all that and you corrected the *hour*.”
He remembers it: her porch light, her bare feet on the boards, and his own voice saying *before midnight*, as if the hour were the thing that mattered. He wishes he didn’t.
“You never lied once,” she says. “Not one line. I’ve been lied to by professionals. I know what it looks like. You don’t have it in you.”
Up close her eyes are red at the rims, and so, he would guess, are his.
“You look like hell,” she says.
“Yeah.”
“Good.” And then, before the word has finished landing: “You didn’t cheat. I know you didn’t.”

body.text: “You said you’d never do that to me. I believe you. That’s the worst part.”
body.else: “You said nothing happened. I believe you. That’s the worst part.”

body: He nods. It was her word to take back, and she has taken it back herself.
The cap of her pen is chewed flat at the end. In January it wasn’t.
“So you owe me.” She lays her pen across her page, square. “You’re going to sit somewhere and explain it until I understand it. Slowly.”
It’s the most reasonable thing anybody has said to him all week.
“Tuesday and before,” she says. “Nothing after. I’m not there yet.”
“Tuesday and before,” he says.
She nods, and picks her pen up, and puts it down again.

Down at the front the doors bang open on the 12:30 section, a TA first with a cardboard box of blue books on his hip, which he drops on the lectern with a smack that carries up to the exit sign. Hale’s seminar is at one, across campus. In forty minutes Lena will sit down at the window end of the oak table and look up the length of it at his chair under the clock. Skye stands and gets her bag onto her shoulder.
“Car.”
His eyes go past her down the side stairs, to the open doors and the lawn outside with its benches in the sun.
“I’m not crying on a bench,” she says. “The internet has a camera.”

choices.text: “Okay. As long as it takes.”
choices.key: When Skye said you owed her an explanation, you told her you’d give it as long as it took.
response: “Okay,” he says. “As long as it takes.”
“That’s the first thing you’ve said I didn’t have to pull out of you.”
She goes down the side stairs and he goes down behind her. On the way he gets the RAZR out of his pocket and holds the red key until the little outside screen goes dark, and puts it back.
At the side door she holds it for him with her hip, as she’d hold it for anybody, and lets it go once he’s through.

choices.text: “I owe you. I know.”
choices.key: When Skye said you owed her an explanation, you told her you knew you did.
response: “I owe you,” he says. “I know.”
“Good. Then we agree on one thing.”
Going down the tiers behind her he turns the phone off in his pocket by feel, and the outside screen goes dark against his palm.
At the doors the noon comes in at them white off the concrete, and her sunglasses come down out of her hair onto her face.

choices.text: *Stand up and follow her.*
choices.key: When Skye said you owed her an explanation, you stood up and followed her to her car.
response: He stands, and gets his bag, and goes down after her.
Halfway down he takes the phone out and turns it off and puts it away again, and doesn’t look at what was on it.
She doesn’t turn round on the stairs to check that he’s behind her. She goes out the side door into the sun as if there were never any question he would be.

s09.slug: THURSDAY · 12:40 PM · THE SAAB, LOT 22 BY THE LAGOON — SLOWLY
body: Lot 22 is the far one, down past the dorms on the Lagoon, half empty at this hour. The white Saab is nosed in at the end of a row with its bumper to the railing and the water beyond it. She unlocks it with the key, not the button, and gets in, and he gets in the other side. She doesn’t start it. She doesn’t turn on the radio.

Through the windshield the Lagoon lies flat and brown-green in the sun. A raft of coots is working along the near edge, black, with white bills, going under and bobbing up. A jogger goes by on the path in a Marisol Track shirt, her ponytail going like a metronome. On the far bank the eucalyptus stand with their roots in the water. On the dash is a new paperback Catechism with a receipt sticking out of it for a bookmark.
The car is quiet. Somewhere behind the dorms a leaf blower starts up, and works its way along a wall, and stops.
She puts both hands on top of the wheel. “So,” she says, bright, “tell the folks at home a little bit about yourself —” She stops. Her hands come down into her lap. “No. Not today.”
The coots go under, and come up.
“Go,” she says.
He goes. Mardi Gras and the levee, and the stopping; what they said on the levee, that they’d each end it, to each face, before anything; Lena on the Sunday; him on her porch on the Tuesday —
“Slower.”
He stops. He starts again at the levee, slower, and makes it to the coat.
“Again.” She’s looking at the water. “Not from there. That’s where it happened. That isn’t where it starts. What does he *want* in this scene?”
“Who?”
“The guy on my porch. What does he want?”
“Not to lie to you.”
“That’s what he doesn’t want. Anybody can play what they don’t want. What does he *want*?”

He looks at the coots for it. He has had the levee, and the van, and every night since on his step, and it should be ready by now, and it isn’t; it comes as it came on her porch, in pieces, except that this time she has told him to take as long as it takes, and so he does.

“Since August,” he says. “The first week. Before I knew you. She was with somebody, and then she was with somebody else, and I told myself that was the end of it, and I believed me. I’d have sworn on anything it was over by the time I met you.” He makes himself keep going. “It wasn’t over. I didn’t know that till the levee. That’s the truth, and it isn’t a good one.”
“What does she want?” Skye says — and then, fast, before he can get his mouth open: “No. Don’t. I don’t want her in the car.”
“When did you know?”
“The levee.”
“Not before.”
“Before, I didn’t let myself look at it.”
“That isn’t the same as not knowing.”

He doesn’t argue it. She was in Burnaby with glue on her neck and he was on a levee in Louisiana, and before that, all winter, he was right here, and in every one of those places some part of him knew, and kept its head down.

body.text: “Explain *you look at me*.”
body.else: “Explain the part where I look at you.”

body: “At Mass,” he says. “You’d turn in the pew and look at me. To see what it was doing to me. To see if I was all right. I never had anybody look at me like that, in there or anywhere else, and I loved it. She doesn’t turn around. She’s already looking at the same thing I am, for her own reasons. She’d be looking at it if I wasn’t there.”
Skye doesn’t say anything. Her face is to the water. Then, to it: “You had a whole winter of pews to tell me that. And you told me on my porch.”

He takes that, and doesn’t try to give it back. Then, because she asked for slow: “My dad and me,” he says, “under the hood of the truck. Two hours, the light on the cord, and he doesn’t look at me, and I never felt closer to him in my life. We’re both looking at the engine.” He stops, and goes on. “I want my life pointed at God. All of it. And I want the person next to me pointed there too — not because I am. On her own. That’s the best I’ve got. It’s more than I had on your porch.”
“And I was looking at you,” Skye says.
“Yes.”
“I thought that was the good part.”
“It was the good part.”
His mouth is already open on the rest of it, and she turns her head and looks at him.
“You still love me. Don’t say it. I can see it. It’s my job.”
He closes his mouth.
Across the water and the roofs, Ferrer Tower strikes one, flat bell and all.
“There’s water in the back,” she says, after it. “If you want water.”
“No.”
“Me either.” She picks at a thread on the sleeve of the navy sweater, and leaves it.

body.text: “You said it’s the one you can say,” she says. “Say why you can’t say the other one.”

body: “Because I haven’t said it to her. I won’t say it to you first.”
Out on the Lagoon the coots go down all together, as if somebody had pulled a plug, and come up scattered.
“That’s an answer,” Skye says.
“What’s the scene about?”
“Me telling you the truth too late.”

“That’s what happens in it. What’s it *about*?” She doesn’t wait for him. “I’ll tell you what I had, around the fifth night. It’s about a guy who’s scared of being happy. He gets the thing, and he can’t stand having it, so he goes and finds a reason.”
“No.”
“Then what.”
He looks at his hands for it, the cracks across the knuckles from the Hobart that won’t heal till May.
“It’s about what I’m for.”
“That’s a hell of a thing to say to a girl in her own car.”
“I know.”

She turns in the seat, her back against her own door, so she can see all of him. “Here’s mine. I went to Mass. I sat there with no idea when to stand up. I learned the words. I learned both endings of the Our Father in this car, on the 101. And I didn’t do any of it *at* you. I did it *with* you. I was happy, and you were happy — I’ve got that on tape, I watched it every night, you were *happy*.” She stops, and gets it back. “So tell me what kind of God looks at that and takes it away.”
What he has is the truest thing he’s got.

“He didn’t take it,” Jack says. “I did. I gave it back. I’d have spent the rest of it lying to you — not with my mouth. With the rest of me. Kneeling next to you facing one way, and you not knowing which. I’d rather lose you than do that to you.”
“That’s not good enough.”
“No,” he says. “It isn’t.”

“Say it’s all true,” she says. “Say I’m wrong and he’s up there. Then he made me too. Like this. Somebody who can’t look at anything without turning round to see what it’s doing to the person next to her. He made that. And then he takes the person.”
He has nothing for that. He looks for something and there isn’t anything.
“I don’t know,” he says.
“You always know.”
“Not that one.”
She looks at him for that, and then out at the jogger coming back the other way, slower now, her ponytail flagging.
“Did you see the blog?”
“I heard it.”
“‘Couldn’t handle her fame.’” Her mouth goes crooked at one side. “I laughed for the first time in a week. Then I threw up.”
It gets a laugh out of him, a short ugly one he didn’t know was in there, and something close to one out of her.
“Sol printed it out,” she says. “It’s on the fridge. Under the lobster magnet. She thought it would help.”
“Did it?”
“A little. Don’t tell her.”
It doesn’t last. She looks down at her hands.
“Did you notice I stopped doing voices? On the phone. Since Ash Wednesday.” She turns one hand over and looks at the palm, at nothing on it. “I gave up the first take. For Lent.”

s09a.slug: THURSDAY · 1:40 PM · THE SAAB — A PARADE
body: “I meant it for you,” she says. “That was the idea. Something you do, that I could do too. Give something up.” She closes the hand. “It turns out you can’t give something up for a person. It doesn’t hold.”
A girl on a bike goes by on the path with a cello case on her back, and Skye watches her out of sight.

“So that’s over. Except I’m still doing it. The phone rings and I say *hi*. My agent. My mother. Sol, from the kitchen, on the house phone, which is insane. My agent thinks I’m depressed. My mother thinks I’ve joined something. *Hi.* Every time. And I don’t know who for.” She looks at him. “Isn’t that stupid.”

Before Lent, every call of hers started with somebody else. A flight attendant asking him to return his seat to its upright position. A Texas Ranger with a warrant. Once, from a makeup chair in Burnaby, a waitress at a Youngstown diner so exact he’d laughed till he had to pull off the road.
He keeps still in his seat.
“Are you still not smoking?” she says.
“Still not.”
Her eyes go to the breast pocket of the Carhartt, and away again, out to the water. “I hate that I’m proud of you.”
Across the roofs Ferrer Tower strikes two.
She waits for the last of it to go out over the water before she says anything else.

body: He starts it twice, and neither one comes out, and he has to start it a third time.
“Somebody I’d have done anything for,” he says. “Except lie to.”
She takes it. She doesn’t tell him whether it’s enough. Her chin goes up a little, and down.
“You can’t even give me a bad one,” she says, and crosses her arms over the navy sweater, and looks at the water.

“A parade,” she says. “I keep going back to it. Somebody’s coat on St. Charles, in the cold, and floats going by. I’ve read it fifty ways. There’s nothing in it. It’s the smallest scene I ever heard of.”
She looks at him.
“I just thought I’d be better than her at something. Explain to me, slowly, why it took you a parade.”
