s09b.slug: THURSDAY · 2:05 PM · THE SAAB — DIFFERENT DEPARTMENTS
body: She cries.
It isn’t loud. Her face goes, and then her shoulders, and she puts the heel of one hand against one eye and then the other, and it keeps coming.
“Glovebox,” she says.

He opens it. Registration in a Ziploc, a tire gauge, a parking stub from the Paramount lot, a travel pack of Kleenex. He sets the Kleenex on the console by the gearshift and shuts the glovebox, and she goes through three of them, and then a Del Taco napkin out of her door pocket, and when that’s gone, the cuff of the navy sweater pulled down over her fist.
She talks through some of it. Not much of it is to him.

“I had a plan,” she says, wet. “For today. I was going to do this in the hall in four minutes and walk away and make you watch me walk away. I had it all —” A Kleenex. “That was the plan. I told Sol this morning I wasn’t even going. I had my keys in my hand when I said it.”
And a little later, into the cuff: “Don’t say anything. I mean it. Not one nice thing.”
Once she laughs, a small broken sound, at nothing he can see. “I did my *eyes*,” she says, to the cuff. “For this. Forty minutes.” And goes on.

Jack isn’t doing well with himself. His hands are on his knees and won’t stay there. The right one goes up to the Carhartt on its own and finds the pack through the canvas, the hard corner of it under his palm, and presses.
There’s a thing he could say that would make this hurt her less. He can feel the shape of it, three or four of them, all easy, all ready in his mouth, and every one of them is a lie.

He did this. He did it on purpose, and he would do it again, and she is crying in her own car with the sleeve of her sweater over her fist; both of those are true, and there’s no way to set them down side by side that makes either one of them any smaller.
Something has hold of his throat. He sits in her car with it. One tear gets out of him and goes down beside his nose.
He doesn’t reach for her. She’s sitting with her back to her own door and her knees drawn up onto the seat and the sleeve over her fist, and all of it says not to.
It goes on a long time. It goes on less. Then it stops, mostly, and she blows her nose, hard, a honk nothing like anybody on television, and balls the Kleenex up in her fist and holds onto it.
The Lagoon has gone a darker green with the sun round behind them. The light has come in across the dash and lies on her knees and his.
“I understand it,” she says. “I don’t accept it. Those are different departments.”
“Okay.”
“Don’t *okay* me.” But there’s nothing behind it. She wipes her face one more time with the cuff and looks at the cuff and pulls it straight. “I’ll respect what you said. I always do.”
He waits.
“But this isn’t done.” She says it to the windshield, and then she turns her head and looks at him until he nods.
“Tuesday,” she says. “Pair 41. Fenner doesn’t take requests.”
“I know.”
“Bring your notes.”
“I’ll bring them.”
“I’m keeping your shirt.”
“It’s yours.”
She puts the key in the ignition and doesn’t turn it yet.
“Text me when you —” he says, and stops.
She looks at him. Her face is a wreck, and she lets him see it, all of it, and doesn’t look away.
“Get out of my car, Costigan.”
She is still holding the Kleenex ball.

He gets out. The air off the Lagoon is cold after the car. He shuts the door and steps up onto the curb, and the Saab starts, and backs out, and goes up the row and out of Lot 22, and doesn’t wait at the stop sign.
Jack stands on the curb with his hands at his sides and the cold coming off the water, in the space where her car was.

s09c.slug: THURSDAY · 2:40 PM · THE LAGOON PATH — THE PACK
body: He doesn’t go back the short way. He takes the path round the far side of the water, under the eucalyptus, past the kayak racks and the little footbridge, while across campus his chair under the clock sits empty through all of 109H.

By the footbridge it comes back. Not the hands; the hands have been better for days. The want. It comes back whole, for the first time since her porch: the first one of the morning on the back step on Glenwood with a cup of Folgers, the scratch and the flare, the smoke going down and doing what it does. There is one thing on God’s earth that would make the next ten minutes of his life go faster, and it’s in his pocket, and he wants it more than he has wanted anything since Ash Wednesday. His mouth waters for it, actually waters. The afternoon is bright and cold, the eucalyptus giving off menthol and cat and last week’s rain, the Lagoon full of light, and none of that is any use to him at all.

The pack is out of the pocket before he’s decided anything. Marlboro Reds, the El Paso tax stamp, the cellophane and the seal, the corners gone soft from two weeks riding against his chest. He stands on the path with his thumb on the little red tab of the tear strip.

response: It goes back in the pocket and he does the button up over it, and walks. Past the footbridge, up the stairs by the dorms, across the lawn. On Delgado’s front steps he takes the phone out and turns it on, and sits down on the top step while it thinks about it.

response: *Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.* On one step and on the next. Round the rest of the Lagoon, up the stairs by the dorms, across the wet lawn. Somewhere around the kayak racks the pack has gone back in the pocket; he couldn’t say when. In the lobby, under the mailboxes, he turns the phone on, and finds he has stopped praying only when he hears it start up.

body: He spent the two hours after that there, with Fenner’s textbook open face down on his chest to the chapter on waves, not reading it, while the window over the desk went from white to gold to the deep blue it goes before the lights come on.

At ten past six he gets up and goes down. Two floors, before he knows what he’s going to say. The stairwell is between suppers, somebody’s microwave popcorn coming down from three, a door on four letting out a burst of television and taking it back.

She’s on her step. The jean jacket, a sweater under it, her hair down; three pages in Hale’s handwriting on her knees with her pencil laid across them. She hears his boots on the flight above and turns the pages face down on her knee, and moves over.
He sits. The concrete is cold through his jeans. On the landing below the wired glass in the door on two has gone dark, and shows the two of them sitting there under the tube light, small.

“Three pages,” she says, with her hand on them. “On how to beat him. In that handwriting that leans back like it’s leaving. And he wouldn’t look at me while I read them. He stood at the window with his back to me like a man watching a pot.” She turns a page over. “And today he asked where you were. In front of God and Caleb.”
“Ohio,” he says.

“Ohio,” she agrees. She looks at him sidelong. “He asked was that the entire state, Miss Broussard, and I said yes, sir, the entire state, and he let it go. I don’t know what he saw on my face. Whatever it was, he let it go.” She runs the pencil along the edge of the pages. “Your chair was empty under the clock all afternoon. I know because I looked at it all afternoon. Caleb asked me was something wrong with the clock.”
It nearly gets a laugh out of him.
“You didn’t answer my question,” she says.
“Which one?”
“Are you all right.”
“I’m good.”
“Don’t you *I’m good* me.” She says it low. “Not tonight.”
“No,” he says. “Not really.”
She waits after that. She doesn’t ask anything else. She sits, and leaves the rest of it to him.
“Skye came back to class today.”
Lena’s pencil stops on the edge of the pages.
“Is she all right?”
“No. Better than the porch.”
She nods, slowly, and is quiet.

“She was in her seat when I got there,” he says. “Before me. She didn’t say a word till Fenner let us out.” He stops, and makes himself go on. “She talked to me after. Two hours. In her car, down by the Lagoon. That’s where I was.”

Lena doesn’t say anything for a little. She straightens; he feels it more than sees it, through the shoulder of the jean jacket against his. She lays the pencil in the fold of Hale’s pages and sets her hands on them.
“I mind. I’m telling you I mind so I don’t have to act like I don’t.”
She says it to his face, with her chin up, and she doesn’t put a joke on the end of it to carry it off.

He would have done a great deal not to be the reason she had to say that. He is the reason. She said it anyway, on her own step, on a Thursday, with Hale’s notes on her knee. He wants to put his hand over hers on the pages, and doesn’t know yet whether he has the right.

Lena hears *it isn’t done*, and he watches it go in. She puts her hands on her knees and sits up straight with it, and doesn’t look away from him.
“All right,” she says. She looks down the flight. “Saturday stands.”
Her hand comes down over his on the cold step, and he turns his over under it.

When she gets up to go in she bends first and puts her forehead against his, cool, the medal swinging forward on its chain; then she goes down to her landing and through the door on two, and leaves it standing a little open behind her.

She takes her time. She asks one thing. “Did you tell her the truth?”

“Then that’s all I need.” She tucks the pencil behind her ear and gathers Hale’s pages. “Seven-thirty, Saturday. And I still don’t know where.”

s11.slug: FRIDAY · 7:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE THIRD FRIDAY
body: By seven the light is gone off the hill. From inside, the dalle-de-verre has nothing left of the day to work with and holds only what the side lamps give it, a deep blue at the bottom of each window going to ink at the top, and over all of it the Douglas-fir ribs go up out of the walls and meet in the dark. Somebody has propped the side door onto Ocean Road with a kneeler, and the cold comes in low along the tile with the sound of the surf behind it.

body.text: Bread and water since morning, his and hers, and all day not a word about it from either of them.
body.else: He had his meatless lunch at the Commons, grilled cheese and the tomato soup. Her bread and water stands alone, and she hasn’t said a word about it all day.

body.text: At noon on the Hollis steps she tore her heel of bread in two and gave him the better end this time.
At noon on the Hollis steps she raised her heel of bread to him first.
At noon on the Hollis steps she said “Seven.” before he could.

body: Father Osei comes out of the sacristy in the purple stole behind the processional cross and its two candles, and at the first station he reads the name off the carving, *Jesus is condemned to death*, and says, “We adore you, O Christ, and we praise you,” and forty people go down on one knee on the tile and give it back to him: “Because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world.”
Lena is on one knee beside him for it.

She came in at five to seven with the black lace already over her hair and sat down in his pew without looking at him, and when the cross turned toward the first station she stood when he stood. Now she is at his elbow at the back of the crowd, her shoulder not quite touching his arm, her booklet held low enough for him to read off it. He has his own booklet. He reads off hers.

Between the stations Gus Ferreira gives a chord from the loft, and the forty walk to the next carving singing the old verse, *At the cross her station keeping, / stood the mournful Mother weeping*, with Gus underneath all of them on the low notes like a keel. Lena sings it a little ahead of the beat in a clean alto. At each station she goes down on the tile without a hand on anything and comes up the same way, and the lace swings forward and back, and every time they kneel the sleeve of her coat brushes the sleeve of the Carhartt, wool on canvas, and every time they stand it doesn’t.

Father Osei reads the meditations short and unhurried, his eyes on the carvings and the page, and takes the corners slowly on the bad leg. The fast has made everything in the church louder in a way Jack is getting used to: the kneelers knocking, the forty booklets turning their page together, the little tick of the candle wicks as the acolytes walk them.

They go down the south wall, the second and the third and the first fall, and round under the sanctuary lamp, and up the north wall, where the carvings are darker. Fifty Lents of candle smoke have got into the grain on that side, and the faces are harder to make out, and he has to look longer at each one to find who is who: the soldiers, the women, the man under the beam.
Somewhere along the north wall, one of the carvings takes hold of him and won’t let go.

choices.text: *The sixth: Veronica wipes his face.*
response: In the carving a woman has pushed in between the soldiers with a cloth held out in both hands, and his face is on it. Father Osei reads that she wasn’t asked, and did it anyway, and kept the cloth.

Jack kneels and asks for nothing. He holds things up instead, one after another, and leaves them on the cloth: Ma at the kitchen table with the long cord; Hale at a window with his back to a room; a white car in a lot by the lagoon, and the face in it. He leaves each one there. The cloth takes what it takes.
The cross turns toward the seventh and the verse starts again, and they go with it, and round the walls, and out.

choices.text: *The ninth: he falls the third time.*
response: The ninth hangs low on the wall by the confessionals: him down on his hands under the beam, for the third time, and the beam on top of him. Father Osei reads it in two sentences and lets them kneel on it.

Jack knows something about the third time. It isn’t the falling. Anybody falls. It’s getting up when you have done it twice already and know exactly how far down the floor is. He kneels on the tile and asks for that, the getting up, and doesn’t ask to be spared the floor.
The church gets up. He gets up with it.

choices.text: *The eleventh: and nothing to think at all.*
response: *Jesus is nailed to the cross.* Father Osei reads the meditation and stops, and the church kneels, and the side door knocks against its kneeler in the wind.

Jack kneels with nothing in his head. All week there have been words in it, on the Hollis steps and on her landing and over the dish machine, sentences going round like plates on the rack, and at the eleventh there isn’t one. He lets it be that. Beside him Lena has her eyes shut and her hands together under her chin.
From the loft Gus comes back in on the low note, and the forty get up off the tile.

s12.slug: SATURDAY · 7:05 AM · THE ANCHOR — DON’T ORDER THE DUCK
body: By five past seven on Saturday the fishermen have the counter from Merle’s stool in, caps on, elbows down, paying cash. Jack has the Hobart. The first rack of mugs goes in with a roar and comes out in a cloud.

Last night on the steps of St. Brendan’s, with the church emptying onto Ocean Road behind them, he told her again to wear something she could walk in, and she took the lace off her hair and said, “I’ll wear what I like, Costigan.” At the bottom of the hill he said *five to seven*, and she said, “Laney says she will *receive* you,” in Laney’s voice, every vowel of it, and walked the rest of the way with her hand in the side pocket of the Carhartt, turning one of Gloria’s gumbands round a finger.

The talk at the counter is last Saturday’s talk, a week on and quieter. Chile. A cousin of somebody’s in a town down there whose name the man can say and Jack can’t, and the church at home taking up a second collection, and the radio’s numbers, which are the radio’s business.
On the shelf over the grill Rudy’s radio is on the Saturday boleros out of Oxnard, a man singing slow in Spanish over strings, and Rudy cracks eggs to it two at a time, one-handed.

Gloria comes down the counter with the grease pencil out of her hair and writes the morning’s pies on the glass of the case in her square capitals, PECAN · APPLE · CHOC CREAM, and stands back from it with her arms folded until she’s satisfied none of them is lying.

body.text: Then she goes to the pass and comes back with a plate, two eggs over and potatoes and a short stack, and sets it on the steel by the Hobart before he has said a word. “Eat.” It’s breakfast, not a thank-you, and she stands there with the rag over her shoulder until he picks up the fork.
body.else: “You look like a man with a jacket problem,” she says on her way past, and comes back from the pass with a plate, two eggs over and a short stack, and sets it on the steel in front of him. “Eat.”

body: When she comes back for the plate it’s clean. She takes it and doesn’t go.
“Tonight?”
“Tonight.”
“What are you ordering?”
“Something French.”
“What time?”
“Seven-thirty.”
She nods at that. It seems to be the one thing he has got right so far.
Gloria looks at him, at his face and at his hands going in and out of the rack.
“Don’t order the duck,” she says. “Nobody can eat duck nervous.”

body.text: At nine, when the fishermen have gone back down the ramps and the counter is a row of empty mugs, she takes Rudy’s brown off its hanger by the register and sits on the end stool with it across her knees and the butter-cookie tin open beside her. She hems the sleeves fast, a row of pins in her mouth, and her coffee goes cold at her elbow and she lets it. When Jack comes round the end of the counter with his wallet out she doesn’t take the pins out to say no; she shakes her head at the sleeve. At the end she bites the thread and holds the jacket up by the shoulders, the whole brown length of it. “Chocolate cream,” she says. “Doesn’t win on looks. Everybody finishes it.” Rudy, who has watched the whole hem from the grill, flips two eggs. “Mijo. Don’t spill on it.”

When the fishermen have gone she comes back along the counter with the rag. “You find a jacket?” He tells her: Theo’s, navy, Italian, so light it’s hardly there, and tight across the back. Gloria wipes the same foot of steel for the length of it. “French silk,” she says. “Pretty. Rich. Don’t take it out in the heat.” She goes off down the counter with the rag before he can ask what that means.

When the fishermen have gone she comes back along the counter with the rag. “You find a jacket?” He tells her: nine dollars at St. Vincent de Paul, brown herringbone, heavy, a dead man’s, a good one. “Walter,” he says. Gloria nods at the name. “Mincemeat,” she says. “Old man’s pie. Nobody young orders it, and it’s the best thing in the case.” She takes the rag on down the counter to Merle’s cup, and fills it without being asked.

s13.slug: SATURDAY · 6:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — THE JACKET
body: The sun has been down half an hour, and the window of 412 has gone a deep clear blue with the eucalyptus black against it and one early star caught in its top branches. Theo’s laptop is shut on his desk. Theo is on his bed on top of the covers in his socks with a paperback face down on his chest, watching Jack get dressed with the attention Frank gives a box score.

The shirt is ironed. He did it at five in the laundry nook at the end of the hall on a board with a scorch mark the shape of Florida, with an iron that spat at him every time he stood it up, and it took forty minutes and a small burn on the inside of his wrist, and the oxford came out flat enough for Ma. In the back of the notebook, under PROPERLY, there are check marks down the side now, one through five, and he has stood over the page twice since six looking at number six to see whether it’s moved.

The Confirmation tie from St. Brigid’s, his only tie, goes on by feel, over and under and through, as Frank taught him at the kitchen table the week before the bishop came. He gets it wrong. He gets it right the second time and leaves it alone.

body.text: Then Theo’s navy, which weighs nothing and fits him everywhere but across the back. From the bed Theo takes one finger off the paperback and points it at the seam between his shoulder blades. He said it on Wednesday. He doesn’t need to say it again.

Then Walter’s herringbone, heavy and brown and easy across the shoulders. Doing up the button he feels the card in the breast pocket through the tweed, stiff, St. Francis and his bird, and he touches it there through the cloth, and leaves it where Walter’s family left it.

Then Rudy’s brown, with Gloria’s hem two inches up the sleeves in stitches so small he has to hunt for them. When it settles on him a faint sweet cologne comes up out of the lining, a wedding in Oxnard a long time ago, and the shoulders still sit a little wide of his own.

body: The envelope with the Anchor money goes into the inside pocket. Number six. The Carhartt stays on its hook on the back of the door with the pack in its breast pocket, and he walks past it.

The roses are on his desk. A dozen, red, long-stemmed, in Albertsons cellophane with a gold elastic round the stems and, square in the middle of the cellophane, a white price sticker: *$19.99*. He bought them at four o’clock on Mission Street, and he has been trying to get the sticker off since. He tries again now with a thumbnail. The corner lifts, and the cellophane under it tears a little, a small clear wound, and the sticker stays on.
“A dozen,” Theo says from the bed. “Red. In cellophane.” He lets the paperback slide off his chest onto the blanket. “You’ve proposed to a bowling alley.”
“They had carnations. Carnations are for funerals.”
“These are what the boy brings in the last reel of a picture that went straight to video. Turn the sticker in. No. *In*. Against you. She’ll find it, but she’ll find it later.”

He turns the sticker in. In the mirror on the closet door there is a man in a jacket and a tie with a dozen roses against his chest, and he looks like a man about to be photographed for the parish directory, and it is going to have to do. He phoned for the cab from the front desk at six, and the sophomore on duty wrote *7:00 DELGADO CIRCLE — COSTIGAN* on a Post-it and stuck it to the phone and wished him luck, grinning. It’s six-fifty. He has the roses in the crook of one arm and his hand on the doorknob, and he stands there, in a borrowed jacket, with a dozen roses, at the door of a room he has walked out of a thousand times without a thought.
Theo has the paperback up again.
“Costigan.” He doesn’t lower it. “She said yes before you bought those.”

He doesn’t stop on her landing. He goes past it and through the wired-glass door onto two and down the corridor under the tube lights, past a door with a Saints flag thumbtacked over its nameplate and a door with a whiteboard that says GONE TO SULLY’S, to 217. He stands in front of it with the roses. He knocks three times, evenly spaced. He practiced it on the inside of his own door at six-fifteen, with Theo watching.

The door opens a foot. Laney Price fills it in a black dress and full makeup, with a hairbrush in one hand held like a microphone. She takes in the tie, the jacket and the roses in one long pass, top to bottom, and shuts her eyes, and opens them again.
“Right on time,” she says. “I could cry.”
She swings the door wide and steps back into the room with the hairbrush up.
“And now,” Laney says, “from the great state of *Louisiana* —”
Lena is standing in the middle of 217 between the two beds, and she has heard every word of that, and has the face of a woman who will deal with Laney later.

She’s in a navy dress, plain, with sleeves to the elbow and a neckline that goes straight across under her collarbones, and it isn’t hers. He knows the box it came in, and the careful upright hand on the label, and at the hem there’s still a faint straight crease where it was folded to fit. Her hair is up off her neck. The medal lies on the navy at her collarbone. She’s in black heels he has never seen, standing in them very carefully, the way you stand on a dock in a swell.
“The shoes are mine,” Laney announces. “They’re half a size small. She will suffer *beautifully*.”
Lena looks at him, and he looks back, and nothing comes.
“You look —” he says.
“So do you,” she says.

He holds out the roses. She takes them in both arms, and the cellophane crackles, and she looks down at them and finds the sticker turned in against the stems where he hid it. He watches her find it. She looks up and says, “Thank you,” very correctly, and turns to look for somewhere to put them, and there is nowhere: both desks are buried in Laney’s makeup, and Coco the coconut has the windowsill.
Laney holds out her arms. “I’ll put them in the sink, sugar. Go.”
Lena draws the roses in against the navy.
“I’m not leaving a dozen roses alone with Laney Price.”
So the roses come too.

The cab is a Yellow Cab idling in Delgado’s circle with its roof light off, and the driver is a heavyset man in a Dodgers jacket. They come down the front steps to it, her hand on Jack’s arm for the heels, and Jack holds the door, and the roses go in first. The meter starts with a click.

They sit in the back very upright, with the roses on her knees and his hands on his, and the cracked vinyl of the seat between her hip and his. The radio is on low. The cab smells of a cardboard pine tree and somebody’s fries, and under that, nearer, of something on her he has never smelled on her before, out of a bottle that has to be Laney’s.
“It’s a pretty night,” Lena says.
“It is,” he says. “Lena, it — it is.”
He hears her name go on the front of it, and doesn’t know what it’s doing there.

Mission Street goes by lit up for Saturday, the Anchor’s windows, the Wharf Rat’s sign with half its letters out; the cab turns onto the wharf, and the planks start under the tires, a long loose drumming, and the lights near the end come up the windshield toward them. Her hand comes off the roses and lies on the seat, on the vinyl. His comes off his knee. The cab stops before either one of them gets anywhere.

s14.slug: SATURDAY · 7:30 PM · LE MARIN, THE HARBOR WHARF — THREE FORKS
body: At night Le Marin is one long room lit from the inside and hung out over the water, more window than wall, and through every window the harbor lies black with the lights of the boats and the town laid on it in long wavering strokes. White tablecloths go down the room in two rows. The glasses stand upside down on them, and every place has three forks. A piano trio is playing low out of somewhere in the ceiling, brushes on a snare and a bass walking along under it.

The man at the stand by the door is in a dinner jacket, silver at the temples, with a reservation book open in front of him the size of a road atlas, and when he says, “Good evening,” Jack knows the voice from Monday. It has a face now, long and kind and entirely serious.

body.text: “Costigan,” the maître d’ reads, and looks up, and says to the waiter who has come to his elbow, very low, “A special occasion.” The waiter inclines his head, barely.

“Mr. Costigan,” the maître d’ says, without looking at the book at all, and in one look round the room Jack understands that the book has been read. The waiter is smiling at nothing. The girl at the coat check is smiling at the coats. In the service door at the back a busboy in a white jacket catches his eye over a tray of water glasses and gives him a thumbs-up, small, at hip height, and is gone. They are all being gently, unbearably kind.

“Costigan,” the maître d’ reads, and there in the book beside the name, in good ink, is the word FORM. He looks up at the two of them. “Will you be dining with the firm this evening, sir?” he asks, with perfect gravity. “No,” Lena says, very politely.

body: The waiter is the man in the white jacket from the window a week ago. He takes them to a table by the window. Jack reaches for her chair, and so does the waiter, and for a moment the two of them have hold of it like men moving a couch up a stairwell, until the waiter lets go, gracefully, and Jack pulls it out, and Lena sits, and he pushes it in a little too far, so that the table meets her at the ribs.
“Thank you,” she says.

She sits very straight with her hands folded on the cloth, and once, and then again, she touches the back of her hair where it’s pinned, to see if it’s still there. She has lipstick on. Since August he has never seen her wear any.

body.text: *A real place, with tablecloths.* He looks at the tablecloth and doesn’t say it. Across the table she sees him look, and doesn’t say it either.
Coming in through the door she said “Form one,” very low, and it has been very quiet since.
At the door she said, “I said yes,” out of nowhere, as though he’d asked again, and he still hasn’t thought of anything to say back.

body: The roses have come in with them and lie on the cloth in their cellophane like a third guest. The waiter, without a flicker, brings a second water pitcher and stands them up in it in the middle of the table, and folds the cellophane, sticker and all, and lays it on the window edge of the cloth, and goes. Now there is a hedge of red roses in the middle of the table, taller than either of them sitting down. He leans left to see her. She leans right. They meet behind the roses, and both of them lean back.

body.text: Then the waiter comes back with a single long-stemmed red rose standing in a bud vase, with the compliments of the house on the occasion, and sets it at Lena’s elbow beside the pitcher, and now there are thirteen, and the hedge is worse.

body: The menus are leather and heavy and say very little.

body.title: Le Marin
body.text: Since 1971 · Sole meunière · Canard à l’orange · Steak au poivre · Bananas Foster, flambéed at your table, for two

body: He has been practicing the French since Tuesday out of a library book with a woman in a beret on the cover, on the bus and over the dish machine and in the shower. Lena reads it without effort, the vowels coming off her in Cajun French and eight years of nuns.

body.text: The waiter offers the wine list to Jack. He opens it, reads one line of something that costs more than Frank’s truck payment, closes it, and hands it back the way Theo taught him, as if he’s read it and found it wanting. “We’ll start with water.” The waiter takes it without the least surprise.
body.else: The waiter offers the wine list to Jack. He opens it, reads one line of something that costs more than Frank’s truck payment, closes it, and hands it back the way a man hands back a parking ticket. “Just water. Please. Thank you.” The waiter takes it without the least surprise.

body: The bread comes in a basket under a napkin, warm, with a dish of butter, and it’s Saturday, and butter is permitted. Yesterday was bread and water. They both look at the bread. They both look at the bread, and then not at each other.
“This is nice,” Lena says.

She says it in the voice she uses on the Newman treasurer: low, sweet, every consonant ironed. He has heard it used on visiting priests, and on a bishop, once, in a receiving line. It has never been used on him.
“It is,” he says. “Lena, it’s very nice.”
“The view is lovely.”
“It is.” He looks at the view. It is the harbor. “Lena, the duck looks good.”
“It does.”
“How’s the Forum?”
“It’s coming along.”
“You’re going to win.”
“Thank you.”
“Hale gave you three pages on himself.”
“That was good of him.”
“It was.”

The waiter comes back with his pad. Jack has had the sentence ready since Tuesday. “*Pour moi*,” he says, “*le canard à l’orange*,” in an accent from somewhere between the library book and Glenwood Avenue, and the waiter writes it down and says, “The duck. Very good, sir,” in English, kindly.
“*La sole meunière, s’il vous plaît*,” Lena says, in French that sounds like French.

The waiter goes. There’s nothing to do with his hands. He lines up the three forks. He moves the third one, the little one on the outside that nobody has ever explained to him, a hair to the left, and back. He can feel the knot of the Confirmation tie whenever he moves his head.

And then a silence comes down on the table, one they have never had: a silence with nothing in it at all. It goes on so long that he hears the trio in the ceiling come to the end of its tune, and the applause of a club somewhere fifty years ago, small and far off, a glass set down somewhere in it, and the next tune start.
He has to say something.

choices.text: *Make a joke about the forks.*
response: “Three forks,” he says. “I figure one’s for the duck, one’s for the fish, and one’s to see if I’m paying attention.”
It lands, perfectly, on the waiter, who has arrived that moment with the water and laughs: a warm, professional laugh, exactly long enough. He fills their glasses. Lena smiles at the tablecloth.
Before he goes, the waiter reaches over, very kindly, and nudges Jack’s third fork back into line with the other two, and somehow that is the worst thing that has happened all night.

choices.text: “You look beautiful.”
response: “You look beautiful.”
“Thank you,” Lena says, in the voice.
They both look at the roses.

He has wanted to say it since the door of 217 opened, and now he has, in a room with tablecloths, and it lies there on the cloth between the bread plates, and neither of them can think what comes after it.

choices.text: “I’ve never had nothing to say to you before.”
response: “I’ve never had nothing to say to you before.”
“No,” she says. “Me neither.”
It’s true, and it doesn’t help. They both hear it go by.
She takes a roll out of the basket that she doesn’t want, and tears it, and butters the bite with great care.

s14a.slug: SATURDAY · 8:35 PM · LE MARIN — BANANAS FOSTER
body: The duck has been in front of him for twenty-five minutes. It came glazed and shining in its orange sauce, half a bird fanned out on the plate like a hand of cards, and it has beaten him. The knife goes in and stops. He saws. The duck slides, sauce and all, toward the rim, and he stops it with a fork, the little outside one, which he understands too late is the wrong one, and it skids the other way and takes a slice of orange with it, and he chases it round the plate.
Between two of the roses he can see half her face. Lena has been eating her sole in small exact bites, and she puts her fork down to watch him.
“This is nice,” she says, and on *nice* her voice is starting to go.

body.text: She reaches round the roses and moves her water glass across the cloth until it stands beside his right hand. “For your hands,” she says. She doesn’t explain it. He doesn’t need her to.
body.else: He gives up on the duck, and puts both his hands under the table on his knees, and leaves them there.

body: Under the table something soft goes over on its side against his ankle, a shoe, and then the other; she has stepped out of Laney’s heels. He shifts his foot to give them room and it comes down on hers, on her stockinged foot, warm through the nylon, and they both pull back under the cloth to their own sides.
“This is nice,” she says, and it cracks clean through the middle.
Lena looks out the window at the harbor.

He can’t see her. He has spent an hour leaning round a dozen roses to get a look at her, and he has had enough of it. He half stands in the borrowed jacket, lifts the roses out of the pitcher in one dripping bunch, lays them back in their cellophane where it lies on the window edge of the table, sticker and all, and sits down.
Now he can see her. She’s right there, in navy, with her hair coming down a little on one side and the harbor black behind her, looking at him. She doesn’t mention the roses. He doesn’t either.
The waiter takes the duck away mostly whole and brings the little dessert cards. Lena reads hers, and her eyebrows go up.
“Bananas Foster,” she says. “In *California*? I have to see what they’ve done to it.”

It comes on a cart: a copper pan over a burner, a dish of butter, brown sugar, bananas split the long way, a little bottle of dark rum with a pour spout, and a box of long matches. The waiter parks it at the window end of their table and lights the burner and goes to work, the butter first, then the sugar, then the bananas laid in to sizzle, with the air of a man who has done this ten thousand times and still likes it. Brown sugar and butter going dark comes up over the table. Lena sits up straight. She watches the pan with her chin up and her eyes narrowed, a judge from Brennan’s brought in to rule.
“He’s going to flame it too high,” she says, low.
“How do you know?”
“Because he’s showing off for me, cher, and I’d do the same.”
It’s the first real thing either of them has said all night, and it’s about the waiter.

The waiter tips in the rum and touches a match to the lip of the pan, and the flame goes up blue and gold, high, higher than it needs to, for the room. At the next table a woman in pearls says, “*Oh*.”

Then the kitchen door swings somewhere behind them and a draft takes the flame sideways, and the end of it licks out over the window edge of the table and finds the cellophane, and the cellophane goes up with a sound like paper, in one bright crackling sheet, the price sticker curling black in the middle of it, and a ribbon of fire runs off it a hand’s width onto the tablecloth.

Jack’s hand is on the roses’ pitcher. He doesn’t remember reaching for it. He throws what’s in it, water and a loose petal and the last of the ice, across the cellophane and the roses and the burning edge of the cloth.
Lena’s napkin comes down on the tablecloth where the ribbon of fire was, and both her hands come down flat on the napkin, pressing, a girl who grew up at a stove.
It’s out. It took four seconds.

body.text: The bud-vase rose has gone over with everything else and lies in the puddle on the cloth, still perfect, pointing at Lena.
When he reached, the seam across the back of Theo’s navy went, one long rip from the collar down, and he can feel the room on his shirt through it.

When he leaned over the table, the card slid out of the breast pocket of Walter’s herringbone and landed on the wet cloth face up: St. Francis and his bird, *In Loving Memory*, Walter J. Pruszynski, lying in the roses’ water beside the black ruin of the cellophane.

When he reached across, the right sleeve of Rudy’s brown went through the edge of the flame, Gloria’s hem from nine this morning and all, and came out again with nothing worse than a scorch along the cuff, and now it smells very strongly of rum.

body: A little smoke goes up off the cellophane, thin and blue, and hangs under the ceiling. The smell is rum and burnt sugar and wet plastic.
The room has stopped. Every fork in Le Marin is down. In the ceiling the trio plays on.

The maître d’ arrives at a speed Jack would not have believed of a man in a dinner jacket, carrying a red fire extinguisher. He looks at the table. There is nothing on it burning. He doesn’t use the extinguisher. He stands at the end of the table holding it upright in front of him in both hands, like a christening candle.

He thinks, very clearly, that he has set the girl on fire, which isn’t true and which he will never be able to explain to Nonna. He looks across at Lena. She is looking at him over the wet ruin of it all: the drowned roses in their blackened cellophane, her napkin, the puddle, the bananas going on quietly in their pan as if nothing had happened. There is soot on one of her knuckles. Her hair has come down on the other side now too.

Her mouth goes first. It goes at the corner and doesn’t come back, and then her shoulders go, and then a sound comes out of Lena Broussard that he has never once heard her make in a public place, a whoop, pure Mid-City, and that sets him off, and then the two of them are gone. They laugh too loud for the room, helpless, past any help at all. She puts her forehead down on the wet tablecloth. He puts his hand over his eyes. Every time it starts to let go of them one of them looks up and sees the extinguisher, and it starts all over again, worse. He tries to say something about the extinguisher and gets as far as *he brought* — and that’s the end of him. She is trying to say something too, into the tablecloth, something with *Brennan’s* in it, and can’t get it out.
The waiter has not left his cart. When it is possible to hear anything again he lifts the little bottle of rum in one hand and the box of matches in the other, and turns to Lena.
“Again?”
Lena wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist.
“Again,” she says.
Jack takes his hand off his eyes. She is right there across the table with nothing in the way, and he can talk now.

response: “I’ve been terrified of you all night.”

“Oh, thank *God*. Me too.” She says it into the tablecloth, and then lifts her head. There’s a damp print of the cloth on her forehead and soot on her knuckle, and she is looking straight at him, and she is entirely herself.
She reaches across the wreck and takes the third fork out of his hand, where it has been all along without his knowing, and sets it down on the cloth, and keeps the hand.

choices.text: “Are you all right?”
choices.key: When the dessert caught fire and you’d both stopped laughing, you asked Lena if she was all right.
response: “Are you all right?”
“I have never been better.” She sits up, wet in the face, and points at him across the table.

response.text: “Look at your *back*.” He reaches round and finds his own shirt through Theo’s navy, from the collar most of the way down.
“Look at *Walter*.” Walter lies face up in the puddle with a rose petal on him. Jack picks him up by one corner and shakes him off, and puts him back in the breast pocket, damp, where he belongs.
“Look at your *sleeve*.” He holds it up: Rudy’s wedding brown, Gloria’s hem, a scorch along the cuff the size of a thumbprint, and coming off the whole arm the smell of the Wharf Rat at closing.

“Costigan, you *menace*.” She points a dripping finger at him across the table, and she is laughing again, not as hard, and her voice is her own voice, all the way back.

response.text: The busboy from the service door appears at Jack’s elbow, sets down two fresh napkins folded into swans, one at each place, and goes away again without a word.

s14b.slug: SATURDAY · 9:05 PM · LE MARIN — THE LAPTOP
body: They eat the first panful anyway. It survived; it sat in its copper through the whole thing, going on in its butter, and the waiter spoons it into two dishes with the gravity of a man serving the last of the rations, and it tastes faintly of smoke and very much of rum, and it is the best thing Jack has put in his mouth since Christmas. The waiter brings two coffees, and wipes out the pan, and does it all again from the butter up. This time the flame goes up a sensible height and comes down, and the room, watching, gives it a small round of applause, and the waiter inclines his head to the room.
Lena tastes the second one with her eyes shut. She opens them.
“Too much cinnamon,” she says. “Brennan’s would *weep*.”
“It’s the same pan.”

“It’s the same pan and a different man’s nerve. The first one he made for the room. This one he made for the fire marshal.” She takes another spoonful, a big one. “Brennan’s has been doing this since before my daddy was born, Youngstown. They light it like they mean it and they put it *out* like they mean it.”
“So it was done properly the first time,” he says.
“The first time it set the table on fire.”
“You just said a thing’s properly done if it’s done like you mean it. He meant it. He meant it all over the roses.”

“I said that about *Brennan’s*.” She points her spoon at him. “Properly is the form, Jack. You can do a thing in the right form and have it go wrong on you, and it’s still been done right. A Mass said by a priest with a head cold is a Mass.”
“So you’re saying tonight went right.”

She opens her mouth and shuts it. She has walked herself, in her mother’s navy dress, straight into the corner, and he can see on her face that she knows it, and he watches her look round the corner for a door.
“I’m saying,” Lena says, “that the *form* was —” She stops. “Lord. You did that on purpose.”
“I had a list.”
“You had a *list*?”
“Reservation. Jacket. Iron something. Flowers. Cab. Pay.”

“And you set fire to number four.” She puts the spoon down so she can laugh properly. “Fine. You win. I hate it, and I want it known that I hate it.” She picks the spoon back up. “Flowers was number *four*?”

body.text: She looks at him over the dish with the spoon in her mouth, and takes it out. “‘Not anybody’s anything,’” she says. “I said it to the mirror for a week.”
She looks at him over the dish with the spoon in her mouth, and takes it out. “‘A dishwasher from Ohio,’” she says. “My mother laughed for ten minutes.”
She looks at him over the dish with the spoon in her mouth, and takes it out. “‘Be with me,’” she says. “I had a speech ready for a no, and you didn’t give me one.”

She sees the card. It’s still lying where it fell, face up on the wet cloth beside the black curl of the cellophane, St. Francis and his bird and *In Loving Memory*, and she reaches over and turns it to the lamp with one finger and reads it. Walter J. Pruszynski. 1921–2009. St. Joseph the Worker. She looks up at the jacket, and at Jack, and puts it together, and her face goes very soft and very interested at once.
“He was in your *pocket*?”
“Nine dollars,” Jack says. “He came with it.”

Lena puts her spoon down and folds her hands on the edge of the table, so he puts his down and folds his. Over the second Bananas Foster in Le Marin, low, with the bananas going cold in their dishes, she says, “Eternal rest grant unto him, O Lord,” and he says, “and let perpetual light shine upon him,” and they both cross themselves. It is the funniest thing either of them has done all year, and neither of them laughs. Walter was born in 1921. He went out to dinner in that jacket, probably, a hundred times, and nobody ever set the table on fire for him.
“He’d have liked the fire,” Lena says, and slides the card across the cloth, and Jack dries it on his napkin and puts it back in the breast pocket where it lives.

body: He tells her he saw it, a week ago Wednesday: Laney coming down the hall with the laptop held out flat, and *Oh my God, Lena*, coming up the stairwell after her. He was on the landing.
Lena sets the spoon down in the dish, carefully, and sits back.

“Then you heard Laney,” she says. “You didn’t hear me. Let me tell it.” And she tells it with her hands. “No knock. There is never a knock. The door just *happens*, and there is Laney Price in the cowboy-boot pajama pants and a T-shirt to her knees, holding the laptop out in front of her flat, like a birthday cake with every candle going, and her BlackBerry in her teeth, *buzzing*, it’s buzzing against her teeth, and she takes it out of her mouth to say, ‘Oh my God. *Lena.*’” Lena does the Highland Park vowels, all of them. “And I said, ‘Laney, I gave it up for Lent,’ and she said, ‘Then *listen*,’ and read it to me. Out loud. With the little broken heart.”
He saw her carry it down the hall. The rest he can see now exactly: the face Laney made when Lena said Lent. He never saw that one.
“And then what?”
Lena looks at the tablecloth. Her hands come down off the air into her lap.

“I sat down,” she says. “On the floor. Between the beds. I had my coat on still, I’d just come in, and I sat down on the floor of 217 in my coat. I don’t know why. My legs did it.” She turns her coffee cup a little on its saucer. “And Laney shut the laptop and sat down on the floor with me. She didn’t say anything. Laney Price. Not a word, for I don’t know how long. Then I got up and went to the five-fifteen at St. Brendan’s, and I lit two candles.”
“Two?”
She looks up at him.
“One’s not your business,” Lena says.

The bill comes in a leather folder, carried by the maître d’ himself. Seventy-one dollars and forty cents. Jack takes out the envelope, Gloria’s gumband and all, and opens it on his knee under the table, and then gives up on the knee and counts it out on the cloth, because there is no other way to do it: fives, and then ones, a great many ones, soft from the tip jar, in a stack beside the coffee cups. Lena watches him do it with her chin on her hand and doesn’t help, and doesn’t look away either.
The maître d’ takes the folder. He glances at the ruined end of the table, at the drowned roses, at the brown stain the shape of Lake Erie where the cellophane went.
“The tablecloth,” he says, without any expression at all, “is on the house.”

He knows whose hands that saucer ends up in at the end of the night. His have been, since September.

Jack gathers the roses up off the window edge of the table, drowned and smelling of rum, and wraps them in a Le Marin napkin because the cellophane is gone. At the door she takes his arm for the heels, and he holds the door, and they go out of the warm long room onto the boards.

s15.slug: SATURDAY · 9:50 PM · THE WHARF, WALKING IN
body: The night has come clear and hard while they were inside. The lamps go down the wharf toward town in a row, each with its own small cone of light on the planks, and past the rail the harbor lies black, and the boats in the marina sit on it with their masts up, and somewhere among them a loose halyard is ringing against aluminum, steady, like a spoon on a glass for a toast nobody gets up to make.

Two boards out from the door Lena stops, puts a hand on his shoulder, and steps out of Laney’s heels. One, and then the other. She picks them up by the straps and hangs them off her fingers, and stands there on the boards in her stockings, two inches shorter, and lets out a sound that has the whole evening in it.
“*Oh*, that’s better,” she says. “Sweet suffering Saint Sebastian, that’s better.”
The planks are cold enough that he can see her feel it. She doesn’t put the shoes back on.

They walk in toward town. The roses go in the crook of her arm, wrapped in their napkin, dripping a little down the navy, and the shoes swing from her other hand, and his hands are in the pockets of the jacket because they have to be somewhere. The boards are uneven. She walks them like she owns them, and every so often her stockinged foot finds a nail head and she says something low in French.
“Tell me the truth,” she says. “The French.”
“Library book.”
“*Which* library book.”

“It has a woman on the cover in a beret. She’s holding a baguette like she’s going to hit somebody with it.” He’s been carrying it on the 11 since Tuesday inside his Oceanography binder so nobody would see. “I practiced on the Hobart. Rudy thinks I’ve been having some kind of episode.”

Lena stops in the middle of the boards and puts the hand with the shoes over her eyes. “*Pour moi*,” she says, in a voice from somewhere between Paris and Glenwood Avenue, deep and slow and terribly sincere, “*le canard.*” And she does the waiter, too, the little bow, the kind English: “The duck. Very good, sir.”
“He was being nice.”

“He was being *heroic*.” She takes her hand down, laughing. “You ordered the duck in French from a man who speaks French, and he let you. That man should be a saint. I’m going to write to the archbishop.”
“You said *s’il vous plaît* like you were born on a boat.”
“I grew up on the bayou, Youngstown. Half of everybody I know was nearly born on a boat.” She puts her arm through his, shoes and all. “It was a heroic duck order.”

Near the foot of the wharf the Anchor’s windows come up on the right, yellow and steamed at the corners, the counter running the length of them and three fishermen on stools with their backs to the harbor. Gloria is behind the counter with the coffeepot. She looks up as they go by. She sees the roses and the shoes and the jacket and the girl in her stocking feet, and she lifts her free hand to the glass, and keeps it there a moment, and goes back to pouring. Jack lifts his hand back. Lena lifts the roses.

There’s no moon. There will be later; there isn’t now. The light is the lamps and the Anchor and, across from it, the bus shelter, lit up white like a fish tank, with a schedule taped inside the glass, and empty.

The 11 comes at twenty to eleven, late, and they haven’t minded. It’s nearly empty: a man asleep against the back window in a Carpinteria Warriors jacket, a woman with a laundry bag between her feet. The driver takes the fare in change and pulls out before they’ve sat down. They sit down anyway, hard, together.

The bus goes up Mission Street under the lights. She turns sideways on the seat, her back against the window, and puts her stockinged feet up on the edge of the seat beside his leg, and leans her shoulder into his. The cold comes off the glass behind her. Her hair has given up entirely now and is down on both sides. She smells of Laney’s perfume and the smoke from the cellophane and rum, and under all of it, of herself.
His hand is on his knee, and it shakes. Not much. He looks at it.
Lena looks at it too.
“Lent?” she says.
“Something else.”

She doesn’t say anything to that. She takes the hand off his knee and holds it in her lap on the navy, on top of the shoes, and the bus goes on up through town, the doors folding open at empty stops and folding shut, past the Mission, past a laundromat lit up with one woman in it folding towels, up the long hill to campus. At the Delgado stop she puts her feet down on the ribbed floor and stands up with the shoes in one hand and the roses in the other, and he gets up after her, and they get off together into Delgado’s circle, her in her stocking feet on the curb, him with his hand out for the shoes she won’t give him.

body: They come through the lobby smelling like a rum cake, the jacket and the girl in her stocking feet with a pair of heels in one hand and an armful of drowned roses in a napkin in the other. The stairwell at eleven on a Saturday is between shifts: the people going out have gone, and the people coming in haven’t yet. The tube light hums over her landing. She kisses him.

He wants her. It is not complicated and it is not quiet, and he stands on the step a little below her with his hand on her face and her mouth on his and the roses wet against his shirt, and it is enough. It is more than he knew to put on a list.

It goes on longer than Sunday on his step. It is not as long as the church steps. When it ends, she ends it, by drawing back not very far, and he hears her take a breath, close enough to feel it, and she stays there with her eyes still shut.
“That was one,” she says.
She opens her eyes.
“Ask me again tomorrow. Properly means not the same night.”

“I know you would,” Lena says. “That’s why it’s tomorrow.” She steps back up onto the landing, and looks at him one more second with the roses against the navy, and goes down the half flight to two.

He stays where she left him, a step below her landing, with brown sugar in his mouth, and listens. Down on two the door of 217 opens on Laney’s voice going up like a siren, and shuts on it. He finds he is grinning at the cinderblock, and goes up the stairs two at a time.

She looks at him a long second, the shoes and the roses in her hands, as if he has answered a question she hadn’t asked yet, and got it right. Then she goes down the half flight to two, and on the turn one of Laney’s heels knocks against the rail, a small bright sound, and she says “*Hush*,” to the shoe, and is through the door. He goes up the two flights to four and doesn’t feel the stairs.

s16.slug: SUNDAY · 7:10 AM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — SOMETHING CAUGHT FIRE
body: Jack has been awake since six, lying on his back on top of the blanket with his hands behind his head, watching the ceiling go from black to blue to the flat clean white of a March morning on the coast, and not thinking about anything you could write down. The eucalyptus outside is full of some bird that has one thing to say and says it.

He can still taste it. Brown sugar, and the cold off a bus window. He has been going over it in order, the way he goes over a shift, from the cab to the landing, and every time he gets to the fire he has to stop, because he starts laughing, alone, on his back, in a dorm room at six in the morning, and then he has to start over from the cab.
The door opens and Theo comes in.

He’s in last night’s good trousers and a sweater, and the trousers are wet at the hems, dark to the ankle, with damp sand caught in the cuffs. He shuts the door behind him with his heel and stands against it and holds up his iPhone, screen out, at arm’s length, like a cue card.

He sees his navy. Jack hung it last night on the back of the closet door, and it hangs there now in the morning light with its back to the room, the seam open from the collar to the hem like a fish on a dock. Theo crosses the room and stands in front of it, and lifts one edge of the split between finger and thumb, and lets it fall. “It died for love,” he says. “I’ll have it buried at sea.”

Third act, the dessert goes up, the roses go up, and a maître d’ in a dinner jacket comes across the room with a fire extinguisher he never uses, holding it out in front of him like a tray of drinks.”
Theo has lain back on his bed with his eyes shut and the phone on his chest. “And the girl?”
“The girl puts it out with a napkin.”
“I’d see it twice,” Theo says, to the ceiling, and smiles with his eyes still closed, as if the joke is going to be there when he wakes up and he wants to save some.

Theo looks at him. Then he falls back on the bed and laughs into his pillow, a long helpless muffled laugh with his shoulders going, and it goes on for some time after Jack has got up.
At the closet Jack knots the Confirmation tie for the 11:30, over and under and through, the same tie as last night. Lifting the knot to his collar, he finds a grain of brown sugar in the fold of it.

s17.slug: SUNDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE FIG TREE
body: The Mary side, halfway up, the aisle end. He’s kneeling when she comes in, and she kneels beside him, and crosses herself, and is quiet, and sits back and puts the lace on her hair, and none of it is an event. It’s Sunday. She is in the pew. A week ago that was a thing he would have walked around for an hour afterward; this morning it’s where she sits.
She’s in flats, and there’s a Band-Aid on the back of one heel above the line of the shoe. He sees it when she kneels.

The church is purple and bare, the flower stands empty, the sun coming blue through the glass and down the fir ribs. Gus brings them up with a Lenten hymn that walks downhill at the end of every line, and Father Osei comes up the aisle behind the cross, and where the Gloria would be there’s only the creak of three hundred people sitting down.

A woman from the Mesa in a camel coat reads Exodus. Moses with the flock, out past the wilderness, and the bush on fire that doesn’t burn up; and Moses going over to look, because who wouldn’t; and the voice out of it telling him to come no nearer. *Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.* And then the name, which isn’t a name, which is *I AM*. The woman reads it in a steady schoolteacher voice and doesn’t try to do anything to it, and it doesn’t need her to.

There’s no Alleluia before the Gospel. Father Osei reads Luke. Some people come to tell the Lord about the Galileans Pilate killed, and the eighteen the tower at Siloam fell on, and he asks them whether they think those people were worse sinners than anybody else, and says no. Then the parable: a man with a fig tree in his orchard that has given him nothing for three years, and he tells the gardener to cut it down, why should it use up the soil. And the gardener says, *Sir, leave it for this year also, and I shall cultivate the ground around it and fertilize it*; and if it bears, good; and if not, then cut it down.
Father Osei comes down to the sanctuary step with his hands folded.

“Notice that the gardener does not ask the owner only to wait,” he says. “A doctor who only waits is not treating the patient. The gardener asks for a year and a shovel; mercy, in this parable, has dirt under its nails.” He goes back to his chair. Behind them somebody approves of the length.

In the prayers of the faithful there is one for the people of Chile, a week on: for the dead and for those still digging, and for the ones waiting for news. *Lord, hear our prayer.* Lena bows her head for that one, lower than for the others, and keeps it down through the response.
Two pews up, on the aisle, Kevin is in his good jacket beside Clare Dominguez. At the sign of peace he turns to her and holds out his hand.
“Peace be with you.”

“And also with you,” Clare says, and then she reaches up with both hands and straightens his collar where it’s gone under on one side, quickly, the way you’d fix a picture going by it in a hall. Kevin lets her.
Lena turns to Jack. Her hand is warm from being folded.
“Peace be with you.”
“And also with you.”
It is a handshake, the same one as last week. Around them the church goes on, people reaching across pews, an old man turning round in his seat to find the family behind him.

After the dismissal, while Gus plays them out, Jack and Lena go down the side aisle together and out through the doors into the courtyard, where the sun is on the olive tree and the coffee urns are steaming on their table and the sprinkler, for once, is off.

They leave the courtyard with a donut apiece in napkins and walk down Ocean Road toward campus. The Grove is on their left, and the noon light comes down through the eucalyptus in coins. A kid on a skateboard goes by them downhill, crouched, and is gone.

Lena eats her donut in four bites without stopping talking. She has opinions about the homily. She thinks Father Osei should be allowed to preach for nine minutes, once a year, as a treat for everybody. She thinks the woman in the camel coat read Exodus better than any lector at home has read anything in the history of the archdiocese. She’s walking a little careful on the heel with the Band-Aid.

“Laney’s shoes,” she says, when he looks at the heel. “I’m sending her the bill from the podiatrist. I’m going to frame the bill.” She hooks her arm through his for the downhill. “I slept nine hours. I haven’t slept nine hours since my Confirmation. I woke up and I lay there and I thought, *he brought an extinguisher*, and I had to put the pillow over my face so Laney wouldn’t ask.”
“He never used it.”
“That’s what *kills* me.”
At the crosswalk by the bike racks, where the light takes its time, she stops and brushes the sugar off her fingers and looks at him sideways.
“It’s tomorrow,” she says.
It is. He has known it since six this morning.

She has scored every gown on the night, and she reads her scores off the back of a Domino’s receipt. Kevin is in the armchair beside the couch with Clare Dominguez on its arm. When the camera finds a gown in the crowd with a train that goes on for some time, Kevin says, “Respectfully, I’d admit that train for observation,” and Clare covers her mouth.
Margot is cross-legged at the end of the couch with her notebook on her knee.

Jack is on the couch, in the middle. Lena is beside him with her flats off and her feet tucked under her, and sometime during the last commercial break, without saying anything, she put her head on his shoulder. It’s there now. Her hair is against his neck and his collar, and he can feel the warmth of her through his shirt, and she is watching the television as if this is how she always watches television.
Not one person says a word about it. Laney, on the floor, turns her head, and sees, and turns back to the screen, and her mouth does something heroic and private all by itself.

Best Director goes to Kathryn Bigelow. The lounge cheers, mostly for Theo’s pool. Margot doesn’t cheer. She watches the screen without moving at all, her pen still in her hand, and her face doesn’t do anything, and Jack, from where he is, can see her not doing it.
